activities.context: When the school bell rang, classes ended. Buses and e-rickshaws waited at the gate. Navya and her grandfather walked to a bus stop where people waited. They boarded. Navya sat by a window and watched outside. As the bus turned, she saw a red postbox. Dada ji said he had once dropped letters into one. A postman collects those letters and brings them to the post office. Workers there separate mail by region. The post office offers other services.
activities.prompt: Dada ji drops a letter into the red postbox. What should the postman do next?
options: Take it to the building where workers separate letters by region.
Give it to the people waiting at the bus stop.
Leave it in the box for passengers to find later.
Take it to the library so the teachers can read it.

why.Give it to the people waiting at the bus: The postman’s job is to collect and carry the letters.
why.Leave it in the box for passengers to fi: The postbox is for dropping letters, not finding them.
why.Take it to the library so the teachers c: The library is not where collected letters are taken.

activities.explanation: The postman carries collected letters to the post office.

activities.context: When the school bell rang, classes ended. Buses and e-rickshaws waited at the gate. Navya and her grandfather walked to a bus stop where people waited. They boarded. Navya sat by a window and watched outside. As the bus turned, she saw a red postbox. Dada ji said he had once dropped letters into one. A postman collects those letters and brings them to the post office. Workers there separate mail by region. The post office offers other services.
activities.prompt: Why does the post office sort letters according to the regions they belong to?
options: Because mail for different areas must be kept apart.
Because waiting passengers must each receive one letter.
Because teachers need the letters to show with their books.
Because the bus must decide where to turn next.

why.Because waiting passengers must each rec: The post office groups letters, not waiting passengers.
why.Because teachers need the letters to sho: The teachers’ books are separate from postal work.
why.Because the bus must decide where to tur: The bus route is not decided by sorting letters.

activities.explanation: Sorting separates the mail according to its region.

activities.context: When the school bell rang, classes ended. Buses and e-rickshaws waited at the gate. Navya and her grandfather walked to a bus stop where people waited. They boarded. Navya sat by a window and watched outside. As the bus turned, she saw a red postbox. Dada ji said he had once dropped letters into one. A postman collects those letters and brings them to the post office. Workers there separate mail by region. The post office offers other services.
activities.prompt: Navya wants to use one of the other services offered by the post office. Where should she go?
options: To the place where workers separate letters by region.
To the gate where buses and e-rickshaws waited.
To the bus stop where people were waiting.
To the postbox where Dada ji dropped letters.

why.To the gate where buses and e-rickshaws: The gate is for waiting for transport.
why.To the bus stop where people were waitin: The bus stop is used for boarding the bus.
why.To the postbox where Dada ji dropped let: The postbox is used for dropping letters inside.

activities.explanation: The post office offers services and has workers sorting letters there.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a postbox and a post office?
activities.answer: A postbox is the box where people drop letters to be sent. A post office is the place where the collected letters are taken and sorted according to their regions. The post office also offers many other services, so it does more than receive and sort letters.
points: People drop letters into a postbox.
A postman carries letters from the postbox.
The post office sorts letters by region.
The post office offers other services.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Dada ji and his brother enjoy keeping in touch. Dada ji writes a handwritten letter to his brother and posts it using the postal service. A reply by letter could take several weeks. To share news sooner, his brother sends an email. Dada ji reads it on his computer, which uses the internet, and they can connect in seconds. Although messages are quick, Dada ji still enjoys receiving handwritten letters.
activities.prompt: If Dada ji's brother had replied only by handwritten postal letter, what would likely have happened?
options: The letter might reach Dada ji after a wait of weeks.
The letter would reach him at once.
The letter would reach him in seconds.
The letter would not reach him at all.

An instant delivery would confuse postal letters with internet communication.
Seconds are possible with internet communication, not posted letters.
Postal letters can be sent and received.

activities.explanation: Postal letters can take weeks to arrive.

activities.context: Dada ji and his brother enjoy keeping in touch. Dada ji writes a handwritten letter to his brother and posts it using the postal service. A reply by letter could take several weeks. To share news sooner, his brother sends an email. Dada ji reads it on his computer, which uses the internet, and they can connect in seconds. Although messages are quick, Dada ji still enjoys receiving handwritten letters.
activities.prompt: What should Dada ji do when he wants to share news quickly but also enjoys handwritten letters?
options: Send an email for quick news and also write a handwritten letter.
Use only the postal service and wait for a reply.
Send an email but never write another letter.
Read the email but keep the news to himself.

why.Use only the postal service and wait for: Waiting for only a postal reply could delay the news.
why.Send an email but never write another le: He does not have to stop writing handwritten letters.
why.Read the email but keep the news to hims: Keeping the news defeats the purpose of communicating.

activities.explanation: This uses fast communication while keeping his handwritten-letter habit.

activities.prompt: Explain why communication is much faster today than it was long ago.
activities.answer: Earlier, communication was slow because letters travelled through messengers, pigeons or the postal service. A handwritten reply could sometimes take several weeks. Today, mobile phones and computers use the internet, so messages, emails and video calls can connect people anywhere in seconds.
points: Earlier messages were carried slowly.
Postal letters could take several weeks.
Today devices use the internet.
Messages and calls connect people quickly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Navya was travelling on a bus when the bus took a turn. After the turn, she saw a fast-moving metro train on a flyover above the busy road. Flyovers help vehicles cross busy roads and crossings and save travelling time. Other flyovers are used by buses and cars. Navya wondered whether these modern facilities could also keep the environment safe and secure, especially because many animals, birds and trees that once lived there are now gone.
activities.prompt: Why could Navya see the metro train quickly after the bus took a turn?
options: Metro trains travel very quickly, and some flyovers carry them.
Metro trains travel slowly, and flyovers cannot carry them.
Every flyover is used only by buses and cars.
Flyovers make vehicles stop at busy roads and crossings.

why.Metro trains travel slowly, and flyovers: This contradicts the speed of metro trains and the use of some flyovers.
why.Every flyover is used only by buses and: This confuses flyovers for metro trains with flyovers used by buses and cars.
why.Flyovers make vehicles stop at busy road: Flyovers help vehicles cross busy roads and crossings rather than make them stop.

activities.explanation: Metro trains travel very quickly, and some flyovers carry metro trains.

activities.context: Navya was travelling on a bus when the bus took a turn. After the turn, she saw a fast-moving metro train on a flyover above the busy road. Flyovers help vehicles cross busy roads and crossings and save travelling time. Other flyovers are used by buses and cars. Navya wondered whether these modern facilities could also keep the environment safe and secure, especially because many animals, birds and trees that once lived there are now gone.
activities.prompt: If the flyover carrying the metro train were no longer available, what would likely happen next?
options: Vehicles would have to cross busy roads and crossings without the flyover's help, and travelling time could increase.
Vehicles would cross the busy roads and crossings more quickly without the flyover.
The flyover would still carry metro trains, buses and cars above the busy roads.
Travelling time would be saved even more because vehicles could avoid the flyover.

why.Vehicles would cross the busy roads and: Flyovers help vehicles cross busy roads and crossings, so losing one would not make travelling quicker.
why.The flyover would still carry metro trai: A flyover that was no longer available could not continue carrying vehicles.
why.Travelling time would be saved even more: Avoiding the flyover would mean giving up its help with crossing and saving travelling time.

activities.explanation: Without the flyover, vehicles would lose its help for crossing busy roads and crossings, and travelling could take more time.

activities.prompt: Explain how flyovers can make travel easier and what Navya could do to help keep the environment safe and secure.
activities.answer: Flyovers help vehicles cross busy roads and crossings and save travelling time. Some carry metro trains, while others are used by buses and cars, making life easier. However, many animals, birds and trees are now gone. Navya could plant trees to help keep the environment safe and secure.
points: Flyovers help vehicles cross busy roads and crossings.
Flyovers save travelling time and make life easier.
Some flyovers carry metro trains, while others are used by buses and cars.
Planting trees can help keep the environment safe and secure.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Some passengers got down at a bus stop close to a hospital. Many people were visiting the hospital, and a banner outside announced an eye check-up camp. Dada ji had brought Navya’s grandmother there for an eye operation. The doctors helped her see better and greatly improved her life. The hospital was an important part of their community.
activities.prompt: Why did Dada ji bring Navya’s grandmother to the hospital?
options: The doctors could treat her eyes and help her see better.
She needed to attend the eye check-up camp with other visitors.
The visit was mainly to use the nearby bus stop.
The hospital wanted more people to visit the community.

why.She needed to attend the eye check-up ca: A camp visit is not the reason given for her operation.
why.The visit was mainly to use the nearby b: The stop was near the hospital but was not the purpose of the visit.
why.The hospital wanted more people to visit: Many people visited, but the hospital did not want visitors for that reason.

activities.explanation: This explains her eye operation and improved sight.

activities.context: Some passengers got down at a bus stop close to a hospital. Many people were visiting the hospital, and a banner outside announced an eye check-up camp. Dada ji had brought Navya’s grandmother there for an eye operation. The doctors helped her see better and greatly improved her life. The hospital was an important part of their community.
activities.prompt: Why was the hospital an important part of the community?
options: It gave care to people who were unwell and helped a grandmother see better.
It was important only because the bus stop was beside it.
It served mainly as a place for the eye camp banner.
It attracted many visitors but did not help them.

why.It was important only because the bus st: The nearby stop helped passengers reach it but was not its main importance.
why.It served mainly as a place for the eye: The banner advertised the camp, but this was not the hospital’s main role.
why.It attracted many visitors but did not h: The hospital did help the people who visited it.

activities.explanation: Its care helped community members, including Navya’s grandmother.

activities.prompt: How is a hospital different from an eye check-up camp?
activities.answer: A hospital is a place where people go when they are unwell and where doctors can carry out an eye operation. An eye check-up camp is an organised event for checking eyes. The camp was being held at the hospital and had been announced on a banner outside it.
points: Hospital provides care for unwell people
Doctors can perform eye operations
Camp organises eye check-ups
Camp was announced by a hospital banner
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Navya’s mother sends money online to Dada ji’s mother for Raksha Bandhan gifts. Dada ji did not have an ATM when he was Navya’s age, so he had to visit a bank and wait in long queues. Navya learns that Money Orders were used to send money through the post office. She also hears that people once used barter, such as exchanging wheat for milk from a shepherd, and that money was invented to make exchanges simpler.
activities.prompt: Navya’s mother needs to send money to Dada ji’s mother again. What is the quickest way for her to send it?
options: Take a Money Order to the post office.
Visit a bank and wait in a long queue.
Send it online with a mobile phone.
Exchange wheat for milk from a shepherd.

Mobile phones can send money online within seconds.
Money Orders send money through the post office, not online within seconds.
Barter exchanges goods or services; it does not send money.

activities.explanation: Dada ji had to visit a bank and wait in long queues.

activities.context: Navya’s mother sends money online to Dada ji’s mother for Raksha Bandhan gifts. Dada ji did not have an ATM when he was Navya’s age, so he had to visit a bank and wait in long queues. Navya learns that Money Orders were used to send money through the post office. She also hears that people once used barter, such as exchanging wheat for milk from a shepherd, and that money was invented to make exchanges simpler.
activities.prompt: Suppose Dada ji had had an ATM when he was Navya’s age. How could he have handled a need for cash?
options: Take out the cash whenever he needed it.
Wait for a Money Order at the post office.
Exchange wheat for milk instead.
Use a mobile phone to take out cash.

why.Wait for a Money Order at the post offic: A Money Order sends money through the post office; it does not provide an ATM withdrawal.
Exchanging wheat for milk is barter and does not provide cash.
Mobile phones can send money online, but they do not take out cash.

activities.explanation: An ATM helps people take out money whenever they need it.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an ATM and a Money Order.
activities.answer: An ATM means Automated Teller Machine. It helps people take out money whenever they need it. A Money Order is used to send money through the post office. In short, an ATM is for taking out money, while a Money Order is for sending money.
points: Explains that ATM means Automated Teller Machine.
Says that an ATM helps people take out money when needed.
Explains that a Money Order sends money through the post office.
Clearly distinguishes taking out money from sending money.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Navya was exploring her neighbourhood with her family. When she saw the rising sun, she used it to identify east. She drew a map with north at the top, so south was at the bottom and west was on the left. The family passed a public library, a post office and a police station, all public places. A nearby park and a shop helped them recognise the area. At a bus stop, Navya checked her map before continuing towards a bus station.
activities.prompt: On Navya's correctly drawn map, the post office is south of the public library. Where should the post office appear?
options: Below the library
Above the library
On the left of the library
At the top of the map

why.Above the library: North is upwards, so this would incorrectly place the post office above the library.
why.On the left of the library: West is on the left, but the post office is south of the library.
why.At the top of the map: The top shows north, but the post office is south of the library.

activities.explanation: South is downwards, so the post office should be below the library.

activities.context: Navya was exploring her neighbourhood with her family. When she saw the rising sun, she used it to identify east. She drew a map with north at the top, so south was at the bottom and west was on the left. The family passed a public library, a post office and a police station, all public places. A nearby park and a shop helped them recognise the area. At a bus stop, Navya checked her map before continuing towards a bus station.
activities.prompt: Why can a park or shop help Navya recognise the neighbourhood during her walk?
options: They can act as useful landmarks.
They show the service provided by every public place.
They always indicate which direction is north.
They make a map unnecessary.

why.They show the service provided by every: A park or shop does not show the services of every public place.
why.They always indicate which direction is: The rising sun can identify east, but a park or shop does not always show north.
Landmarks can help someone recognise a place, but they do not remove the need for a map.

activities.explanation: Landmarks help people recognise a place easily, and parks and shops can be useful landmarks.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Exploring Our Neighbourhood

activities.title: At the School Gate
activities.prompt: Which vehicles were waiting at the school gate?
options: School buses and e-rickshaws
Metro trains and flyovers
Postmen and letter boxes
Hospitals and eye camps
activities.explanation: The school bell had rung. School buses and e-rickshaws were waiting at the gate.

activities.title: The Letter Route
activities.prompt: A postman took letters from the post office to the postbox.
activities.explanation: The route was the other way round. Letters went from the postbox to the post office.

activities.title: The Red Letter Box
activities.prompt: A postman took the letters from the ______ to the post office.
activities.hint: Navya saw a red one from the bus.
activities.explanation: The postman collected letters from the postbox. He then took them to the post office.

activities.title: Ways We Communicate
activities.prompt: Put these communication methods in order from earliest to latest.
items: Mobile phones and computers with the internet
activities.explanation: Good ordering! Communication became faster as new ways were invented.

activities.title: A Helpful Visit
activities.prompt: The doctors helped Dada ji's grandmother see better after her eye operation.
activities.explanation: Dada ji brought his grandmother for an eye operation. The doctors greatly improved her life.

activities.title: ATM
activities.prompt: An ATM means Automated Teller ______.
activities.hint: Say the full name slowly, then read its last word.
activities.explanation: ATM is short for Automated Teller Machine. It helps people take out money.

activities.title: Before ATMs
activities.prompt: Before ATMs, what did Dada ji do at the bank?
options: Wait in long queues
Use an ATM
Send money online
Join an eye camp
activities.explanation: Dada ji had no ATM then. He visited the bank and waited in long queues.

activities.title: Reading Navya's Map
activities.prompt: Which statement matches Navya's map?
options: North is up and west is left.
North is down and west is right.
South is up and east is left.
West is up and north is down.
activities.explanation: The map shows north at the top. Places in the west appear on the left.

chapters.title: Nature Trail
chapters.summary: In this chapter: setting out and forest safety; animals in the forest and by the pond; bird features and bird diary; water animals and tiny animals.

lessons.title: Setting Out and Forest Safety

activities.prompt: What should we remember before stepping into a forest?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Exploring the Forest Safely
activities.body: Your class went on a nature trail at Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh. At the forest entrance, you saw tall trees and chirping birds. Abha Didi, a nature scientist, will guide you. She studies plants and animals. You must not harm forest life. Be careful in new places. Do not tease animals, damage trees or flowers, or throw rubbish. Do not bring pets, firearms, weapons or polythene bags.
keyPoints: The class visited a nature trail at Pachmarhi.
Abha Didi studies plants and animals.
Forest plants and animals must stay unharmed.
activities.explanation: Nature trails help you explore plants, animals and new places safely.

activities.prompt: Students visit Pachmarhi with Abha Didi. How should they explore safely?
steps: Abha Didi studies plants and animals, so she can guide their exploration.
Teasing animals or damaging plants is forbidden because no harm is allowed.
Pets, weapons, polythene bags, and garbage stay out to keep visits safe.
Following her guidance and forest safety rules will protect the forest.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the Place
activities.prompt: Where did the students go for their nature trail?
options: Pachmarhi, Madhya Pradesh
Pachmarhi, Kerala
Pune, Madhya Pradesh
Kochi, Kerala
activities.explanation: The students went on a nature trail at Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh.

activities.title: Match the Forest Facts
activities.prompt: Match each place with what happened there.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows something from the forest visit.

activities.title: Fill in the Blank
activities.prompt: Abha Didi is a nature ______.
activities.hint: She studies plants and animals.
activities.explanation: Abha Didi is a nature scientist. She studies plants and animals.

activities.title: At the Entrance
activities.prompt: At the forest entrance, the students heard chirping birds.
activities.explanation: Chirping birds were seen at the forest entrance.

activities.title: Choose the Safe Action
activities.prompt: You enter a new forest trail. What should you do?
options: Follow Abha Didi
Explore alone
Pick forest flowers
Tease small animals
activities.explanation: Abha Didi will guide you. You should also be careful in new places.

activities.title: Pack for the Visit
activities.prompt: What should you do with a polythene bag before the visit?
options: Do not bring it
Carry it inside
Fill it with rubbish
Carry it around
activities.explanation: Polythene bags should not be brought into the forest.

activities.prompt: The students are on a nature trail at Pachmarhi. Abha Didi will guide them. What should she help them learn about?
options: The plants and animals found in the forest.
The best way to tease birds in the forest.
The best way to damage flowers in the forest.
The best way to bring pets into the forest.

why.The best way to tease birds in the fores: Studying animals does not include teasing, because animals must not be teased.
why.The best way to damage flowers in the fo: Studying plants does not include damaging, because plants must not be harmed.
why.The best way to bring pets into the fore: Studying animals does not include bringing pets, because pets must not be brought.

activities.explanation: She studies plants and animals and will guide their forest exploration.

activities.prompt: The students arrive at a new forest place. They want to touch a small animal. What is the best choice?
options: Watch quietly without teasing the animal.
Pull it closer so they can see it.
Damage a nearby plant to make it come.
Tease it quickly before it runs away.

They think pulling helps, but animals must not be harmed.
They think damaging a plant helps, but plants must not be harmed.
They think teasing helps them see, but animals must not be teased.

activities.explanation: Quiet watching harms no animals, plants, or trees.

activities.prompt: Someone says, "Chirping birds can be teased safely." Why is it wrong?
options: Chirping birds are still animals that must not be teased.
Chirping birds prove that the forest has no animals.
Chirping birds mean that all animals enjoy being teased.
Chirping birds show that visitors may damage trees.

why.Chirping birds prove that the forest has: They mistake chirping for proof that no animals live there.
why.Chirping birds mean that all animals enj: They think happy sounds mean animals enjoy being teased.
why.Chirping birds show that visitors may da: They wrongly connect birdsong with permission to damage trees.

activities.explanation: Birds are animals, so the rule against teasing also applies to them.

activities.prompt: A student has rubbish in hand near a forest path. A bird is chirping nearby. What should the student do?
options: Carry the rubbish out of the forest.
Throw it into the forest after the visit.
Leave it under a tall tree.
Give it to the chirping bird.

why.Throw it into the forest after the visit: Throwing rubbish in the forest is forbidden.
Leaving rubbish under a tree still puts garbage in the forest.
They think birds should eat rubbish, but animals must not be harmed.

activities.explanation: Garbage must not be thrown in the forest, so it must leave.

activities.prompt: Forest birds can be heard at the entrance. The class wants to compare safe ways to watch them. Which test is fairest?
options: Watch quietly and leave the birds and trees alone.
Pull a branch and watch the birds move.
Tease a bird and watch it come closer.
Drop rubbish and watch the birds gather.

Pulling branches harms trees, so it is not a fair test.
Teasing is forbidden, so it cannot be a fair test.
Dropping rubbish breaks the rule against forest garbage.

activities.explanation: Watching and leaving things alone harms no plants or animals.

lessons.sceneAlt: A trail runs through the Serenity Botanical Garden in Gandhinagar, India.
lessons.sceneCaption: A nature trail in a botanical garden where children can learn about natural heritage.

sceneCredit.text: A Trail , Serenity Botanical Garden, Ghandhinagar, India by Ridhdhesh Jivawala, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lessons.title: Animals in the Forest and by the Pond

activities.prompt: What might we discover in the forest and near the pond?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Forest Animals
activities.body: The students travelled to a forest in jeeps. They saw many plants and animals there. An elephant uses its trunk for food and water. A rabbit munches grass near a pond. Forest animals include a sparrow, Indian Giant Squirrel, Spectacled Monkey, gaur, and hornbill.
keyPoints: An elephant uses its long trunk for food and water.
A sparrow has a short, strong beak.
Animals live in the forest and near the pond.
activities.explanation: These animals have special features and behaviours.

activities.prompt: An elephant is near food and water. How can it take both?
steps: The elephant has a long trunk.
A long trunk can reach food and water.
That length helps it take what it needs.
So the elephant uses its trunk to take food and water.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Useful Trunk
activities.prompt: Which animal uses its long trunk to take food and water?
options: Sparrow
Hornbill
Gaur
Elephant
activities.explanation: Its long trunk helps it take both food and water.

activities.prompt: A sparrow's short, strong beak is useful for cracking seeds.
activities.explanation: The sparrow has a short and strong beak for cracking seeds.

activities.title: Fill the Gap
activities.prompt: A ______ uses its long trunk to take food and water.
activities.hint: Look for the animal with a long trunk.
activities.explanation: An elephant takes food and water with its long trunk.

activities.title: Match Each Clue
activities.prompt: Match each animal clue to the right animal.
activities.explanation: Each clue describes something the animal does or has.

activities.title: True Hornbill Clue
activities.prompt: Which statement about the hornbill is true?
options: A large curved beak and a short tail
A short strong beak for cracking seeds
Headgear from its forehead like a horn
A long trunk for taking food and water
activities.explanation: The hornbill had headgear from its forehead. It also had a long tail.

activities.prompt: A child tests a sparrow with seeds. Which test is fair?
options: Offer seeds and watch its short, strong beak.
Offer mud and watch its long trunk.
Offer grass and watch its horn-like headgear.
Offer water and watch its large curved beak.

An elephant's trunk takes food and water, not seeds.
why.Offer grass and watch its horn-like head: Headgear grows on a hornbill, which does not crack seeds.
why.Offer water and watch its large curved b: A hornbill's large curved beak is not for cracking seeds.

activities.explanation: The sparrow's short, strong beak cracks seeds.

activities.prompt: A child sees a strong, buffalo-like animal. Which animal fits?
options: The gaur, because it has shorter horns.
The gaur, because it has a long trunk.
The rabbit, because it munches grass.
The hornbill, because it has headgear.

A long trunk belongs to an elephant, not a gaur.
The rabbit is known here for munching grass, not being buffalo-like.
Headgear belongs to the hornbill, not the buffalo-like gaur.

activities.explanation: A gaur looks like a buffalo and has shorter horns.

activities.prompt: Students find footprints in mud near a pond. A rabbit munches grass there. What can they infer?
options: Animals were near the pond.
The hornbill left the footprints.
The elephant cracked seeds there.
The sparrow used the mud.

The footprints do not prove that a hornbill made them.
An elephant's trunk takes food and water; it does not crack seeds.
A sparrow's beak cracks seeds, but nothing shows it used mud.

activities.explanation: The footprints and the rabbit show that animals were there.

activities.prompt: One bird has a long tail and a large curved beak. Another has a short, strong beak. Which bird is the hornbill?
options: The first bird, because it has a long tail and curved beak.
The first bird, because it has a short, strong beak.
The second bird, because it has a long tail and curved beak.
The second bird, because it has headgear like a horn.

why.The first bird, because it has a short,: A short, strong beak belongs to the sparrow.
why.The second bird, because it has a long t: The sparrow does not have the long tail and curved beak.
why.The second bird, because it has headgear: The hornbill has headgear, but the second bird has a short beak.

activities.explanation: The hornbill has a long tail and a large curved beak.

lessons.sceneAlt: A giant Indian Malabar squirrel sits in sunlight at Pachmarhi.
lessons.sceneCaption: A giant Indian Malabar squirrel photographed in sunlight at Pachmarhi.

sceneCredit.creator: Paras31194

lessons.title: Bird Features and Bird Diary

activities.prompt: How do birds use their beaks and claws?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Some Bird Features
activities.body: Beaks and claws help birds eat and act. Birds have different beaks, claws and eating habits. An eagle has a sharp, curved beak and sharp claws. It catches prey, meaning animals caught for food. A sunbird's long beak drinks nectar from flowers. Close your eyes and listen. Open them and focus on one bird. Observe how it moves, eats and sits. Write observations in a bird diary.
keyPoints: A bird's beak and claws help it eat and do other activities.
Different birds have different beaks, claws and eating habits.
A bird diary records how a bird moves, eats and sits.
activities.explanation: Birds have different features, and a diary records what you observe.

activities.prompt: Why do an eagle and a sunbird have different beaks and claws?
steps: An eagle catches prey, so its sharp, curved beak and sharp claws help.
A sunbird drinks nectar, so its long beak helps it reach the flowers.
Because eating habits differ, beaks and claws also differ.
Therefore, their beaks and claws help them eat and do other activities.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which parts help a bird eat and do other activities?
options: Its beak and claws
Its wings only
Its feathers only
Its tail only
activities.explanation: A bird's beak and claws help it eat and do other activities. Good choice!

activities.prompt: A sunbird has a long beak for drinking nectar from flowers.
activities.explanation: Yes! A sunbird's long beak helps it drink nectar from flowers.

activities.prompt: Match each bird study action to the correct action.
pairs: Watch how it moves, eats and sits
activities.explanation: Close your eyes to listen. Open them to focus. Write your observations in a bird diary.

activities.prompt: A sunbird has a ______ beak for drinking nectar from flowers.
activities.hint: Think about the length of its beak.
activities.explanation: A sunbird has a long beak for drinking nectar from flowers.

activities.prompt: What can you do to focus on one bird at a time?
options: Close your eyes and listen
Open your eyes and focus on one bird
Write about many birds together
Remember only the bird's sound
activities.explanation: Open your eyes and focus on one bird at a time. You will observe it better.

activities.prompt: You watched one bird closely. What should you record?
options: Why the bird moved
How the bird moved, ate and sat
When the bird was born
How many eggs the bird had
activities.explanation: Observe how a bird moves, eats and sits. Then write these details in your diary.

activities.prompt: Birds with different beaks must have the same eating habits.
activities.explanation: Different birds have different beaks, claws and eating habits.

activities.prompt: Match each bird part to its description.
pairs: Help with eating and other activities
activities.explanation: An eagle has a sharp, curved beak and sharp claws. A sunbird has a long beak.

activities.prompt: A bird uses sharp claws to catch prey. Which bird is it?
options: It is an eagle that catches prey.
It is a sunbird that catches prey.
It is an eagle that drinks nectar.
It is a sunbird that drinks nectar.

This mistakes the sunbird's nectar habit for the eagle's prey-catching habit.
This gives the eagle the sunbird's nectar-eating habit.
This gives the sunbird the eagle's prey-catching habit.

activities.explanation: The eagle has sharp claws for catching prey.

activities.prompt: Two birds eat differently. The child says, "They have the same beak and claws." What is the best reply?
options: Different birds have different beaks, claws, and eating habits.
Every bird has a sharp, curved beak for catching prey.
Every bird has a long beak for drinking nectar.
Beaks and claws do not help birds eat or do other things.

why.Every bird has a sharp, curved beak for: This wrongly assumes every bird catches prey.
why.Every bird has a long beak for drinking: This wrongly assumes every bird drinks nectar.
why.Beaks and claws do not help birds eat or: This wrongly says body parts never help birds.

activities.explanation: Different birds can have different beaks, claws, and eating habits.

lessons.sceneAlt: A grey-headed fishing eagle has a powerful grey beak and long black talons.
lessons.sceneCaption: A powerful grey beak and long talons help this fishing eagle hunt.

sceneCredit.text: Grey-Headed Fishing Eagle by Shankar70, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Shankar70

lessons.title: Water Animals and Tiny Animals

activities.prompt: What helps water animals swim, and how do tiny insects explore their world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Special features of animals
activities.body: Water animals have special features for surviving. Fish use fins to swim. A gharial is a crocodile with a long, narrow and pointed snout. Turtles have strong shells and webbed feet. Frogs can live on land or in water. Forest insects include ants, beetles, bees, flies, praying mantises and butterflies.
keyPoints: Fish have fins that help them swim.
Turtles have strong shells and webbed feet.
Frogs can live both on land and in water.
A gharial has a long, narrow and pointed snout.
Ants, beetles and bees are forest insects.
activities.explanation: These special features help water animals survive.

activities.prompt: A turtle swims in a pond. Why can it swim easily and stay safe?
steps: The turtle has webbed feet, so it can swim easily.
It has a strong shell, so it stays safe.
Each feature gives it special help for surviving.
So its feet help with swimming, and its shell helps with safety.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Helping a fish swim
activities.prompt: Which feature helps a fish swim?
options: Fins
Shells
Antennae
Wings
activities.explanation: Fish have fins that help them swim.

activities.title: Animal and feature pairs
activities.prompt: Match each animal with its feature or special place.
pairs: A long, narrow and pointed snout
Webbed feet that help it swim easily
Able to live on land and in water
activities.explanation: The pairs match animals with features or places where they can live.

activities.title: A special snout
activities.prompt: Which animal is a crocodile with a long, narrow and pointed snout?
options: Gharial
Grasshopper
Beetle
Ant
activities.explanation: A gharial is a crocodile with a long, narrow and pointed snout.

activities.title: An insect's legs
activities.prompt: A grasshopper is an insect. It has three pairs of ______.
activities.hint: Think about the insect's six feet.
activities.explanation: An insect has three pairs of legs.

activities.title: Features of an insect
activities.prompt: Which pair of features belongs to an insect?
options: Antennae and three pairs of legs
Webbed feet and strong turtle shells
Fish fins and narrow crocodile snouts
Turtle shells and narrow crocodile snouts
activities.explanation: One pair of antennae and three pairs of legs are insect features.

activities.title: Forest insect group
activities.prompt: Which group contains only animals named as forest insects?
options: Ants and bees
Frogs, turtles and swimming fish
Gharials, turtles and land frogs
Fish, turtles and forest ants
activities.explanation: Ants and bees are named as forest insects. The other groups include animals outside that list.

activities.prompt: An insect cannot use its antennae. What will be harder for it?
options: Sense the world around it.
Swim easily through water.
Stay safe with a strong shell.
Move easily with webbed feet.

This confuses an insect with a water animal.
This confuses an insect with a turtle.
This confuses an insect with a turtle.

activities.explanation: This is right because antennae help insects sense their surroundings.

activities.prompt: A turtle needs swimming and safety features. Which pair is right?
options: Webbed feet for swimming, and a strong shell for safety.
A strong shell for swimming, and webbed feet for safety.
Fins for swimming, and a strong shell for safety.
One antenna pair for swimming, and a shell for safety.

why.A strong shell for swimming, and webbed: This swaps the jobs of the shell and webbed feet.
why.Fins for swimming, and a strong shell fo: This mixes up turtle feet with fish fins.
why.One antenna pair for swimming, and a she: This mixes up turtle feet with insect antennae.

activities.explanation: Both parts are right because feet swim and the shell protects.

activities.prompt: A child calls a gharial a turtle. What makes the claim wrong?
options: A gharial is a crocodile with a long, narrow, pointed snout.
A gharial is an insect with three pairs of legs.
A gharial is a fish with helpful fins.
A gharial is a frog that lives in water and land.

why.A gharial is an insect with three pairs: This mixes up a crocodile with an insect.
This mixes up a crocodile with a fish.
why.A gharial is a frog that lives in water: This mixes up a crocodile with a frog.

activities.explanation: This is right because a gharial is a crocodile.

activities.prompt: A child says all forest animals are alike. Why is this wrong?
options: The forest has many different animal kinds.
All forest animals have three pairs of legs.
All forest animals live in water.
All forest animals share the same features.

why.All forest animals have three pairs of l: This wrongly treats every forest animal as an insect.
This wrongly thinks all forest animals are water animals.
why.All forest animals share the same featur: This wrongly claims that all forest animals are alike.

activities.explanation: This is right because the forest has a wonderful diversity of animals.

lessons.title: Plants, Leaves and Leaf Patterns

activities.prompt: What can leaves tell us about the plants around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Leaf Clues
activities.body: Students collect leaves from different plants. Leaf pictures help identify plants. You can observe leaves in your neighbourhood. Leaves vary in colour, texture and shape. The lines on a leaf are called veins. Leaves can have two different vein arrangements. Each leaf has its own unique pattern. A leaf autograph is a leaf picture made by rubbing a crayon over paper.
keyPoints: Leaf pictures can help identify plants.
Leaves vary in colour, texture, shape and vein patterns.
A leaf autograph shows the shape of a leaf.
activities.explanation: Look closely at leaves and their patterns.

activities.prompt: A child collects a leaf and wants to make a leaf autograph. How should the child do this?
steps: The child places the rough, vein-side upwards, because this is the correct side for a leaf autograph.
The child covers the leaf with plain paper, because the paper will carry the rubbing.
The child rubs a crayon over the paper, because this makes the leaf's shape appear.
The child uses a picture of the leaf to identify and name the plant or tree.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Leaves from different plants can have different colours, textures and shapes.
activities.explanation: Leaves can differ in colour, texture and shape.

activities.prompt: The lines you see on a leaf are called ______.
activities.hint: Look at the lines drawn across a leaf.
activities.explanation: The lines on a leaf are called veins.

activities.prompt: Match each leaf observation or autograph item with its correct word.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a leaf observation or autograph step from your book.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to make a leaf autograph.
items: Cover the leaf with plain paper
Rub a crayon over the paper
activities.explanation: These are the steps for making a leaf autograph.

activities.prompt: You want to make a leaf autograph. Which action makes the leaf's shape appear?
options: Cover leaf with paper
Rub crayon over paper
Leaf in two halves
Wet the plain sheet
activities.explanation: Rubbing a crayon over the paper makes the leaf's shape appear.

activities.prompt: For a leaf autograph, we place the smooth side of the leaf upwards.
activities.explanation: We place the rough, vein-side upwards before making the autograph.

activities.prompt: Which information helps you name the plant or tree to which a leaf belongs?
options: The leaf's pattern
The paper's colour
The room's plants
The crayon's shape
activities.explanation: Leaf pictures help identify plants, and each leaf has its own unique pattern.

activities.prompt: Two leaves have similar shapes. Why might their patterns still be different?
options: Each leaf has its own unique pattern.
Each leaf has the same unique pattern.
Plants give leaves only one pattern.
Veins make every leaf look the same.

This wrongly says the same pattern belongs to every leaf.
This wrongly limits leaves to one pattern.
This wrongly says veins make all leaves look alike.

activities.explanation: Every leaf has its own unique pattern.

activities.prompt: A child wants a leaf autograph. Which steps make the leaf's shape appear?
options: Place the rough side up, cover it, then rub.
Place the smooth side up, cover it, then rub.
Cover it, rub it, then place the leaf.
Rub it first, cover it, then place the leaf.

why.Place the smooth side up, cover it, then: This places the wrong side upwards for the autograph.
This leaves out the correct placement of the leaf.
why.Rub it first, cover it, then place the l: This rubs the crayon before covering the leaf with paper.

activities.explanation: This follows the correct order for making a leaf autograph.

lessons.title: The Web of Life and Nature Challenge

activities.prompt: What happens when one part of nature disappears?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Our Web of Life
activities.body: All living beings are connected with one another. In the yarn game, each player gets a card naming a plant, animal or natural element. One player holds the yarn and thinks about a connection. The yarn passes to the player with the matching connection. As more connections are made, the web grows. If a part disappears, the web weakens or collapses.
keyPoints: Living beings are connected.
Each connection helps the web grow.
A missing part weakens the web.
activities.explanation: Each new connection helps the web grow.

activities.title: Build a food chain

tasks.say: Build the longest chain: grass, grasshopper, frog and snake.
tasks.then: Four living things make four trophic levels, from the producer up to the largest carnivore.

tasks.say: Cut the chain down to just the grass and the grasshopper.
tasks.then: The grass is the producer at trophic level 1; the grasshopper is a herbivore at trophic level 2.

tasks.say: Give the grass the most sunlight you can.
tasks.then: Green plants capture only about 1 part in 100 of sunlight, so from 1000 units the grass stores about 10.

activities.takeaway: A food chain shows who eats whom: green plants are the producer at the first trophic level, each animal after that is a consumer at the next level, energy flows only one way, and less of it is left at each step.
activities.explanation: A food chain shows who eats whom: green plants are the producer at the first trophic level, each animal after that is a consumer at the next level, energy flows only one way, and less of it is left at each step.

activities.prompt: In the yarn game, the tree card disappears. What may happen to the web?
steps: The tree gives the bird food, because the tree provides food for a bird.
Removing the tree card removes that connection from the yarn web.
The web weakens or may collapse, because it has lost a part.
This shows that all living beings are connected with one another.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Connected Living Things
activities.prompt: Which statement is true about living beings?
options: All living beings are connected.
Only trees are connected.
Only animals are connected.
Plants grow without connections.
activities.explanation: All living beings are connected, so plants and animals belong to the same web.

activities.title: Match the Yarn Game Parts
activities.prompt: Match each part with its role in the yarn game.
activities.explanation: These pairs show how cards, connections and yarn make the growing web.

activities.title: A Missing Part
activities.prompt: The web weakens or collapses when a part of it disappears.
activities.explanation: The web weakens or collapses when one of its parts disappears.

activities.title: What Does the Tree Provide?
activities.prompt: A tree provides ______ for a bird.
activities.hint: It is what the bird gets from the tree.
activities.explanation: The tree provides food for the bird.

activities.title: The Growing Web
activities.prompt: The web grows even when a part of it disappears.
activities.explanation: A missing part weakens or collapses the web instead of helping it grow.

activities.title: Prepare for a Nature Walk
activities.prompt: What can you do before a nature walk in a nearby park?
options: Identify yarn colours.
Choose matching players.
Identify plants and animals.
Collect matching yarn cards.
activities.explanation: You can identify plants and animals and study their features before the walk.

activities.title: Order the Yarn Game
activities.prompt: Put the yarn game steps in order.
items: The yarn holder thinks about a connection.
The yarn passes to the matching player.
The web grows as more connections are made.
activities.explanation: Cards come first, then a connection is chosen and shared. More connections grow the web.

activities.title: Focus for the Forest Role-Play
activities.prompt: Which focus should the forest role-play have?
options: Replacing living things with toys
Protecting animals and plants
Keeping every card alone
Leaving the forest behind
activities.explanation: The forest role-play should focus on protecting animals and plants.

activities.prompt: A tree provides food for a bird. If the tree card leaves the yarn web, what may happen?
options: The web may weaken or collapse.
The yarn will grow without the tree.
The bird card will become the yarn.
The players will stop making connections.

This is wrong because losing a part does not make the web grow.
This is wrong because a bird card does not become yarn.
why.The players will stop making connections: This is wrong because losing one card does not stop all connections.

activities.explanation: This is right because the web loses a part when the tree card leaves.

activities.prompt: A player holds the yarn and thinks about a connection. A river supports a fish. Which card should get the yarn?
options: The fish card.
The tree card.
The bird card.
The river card.

This is wrong because the tree matches the bird's food connection.
This is wrong because the bird matches the tree's food connection.
This is wrong because the yarn passes to the other matching card.

activities.explanation: This is right because the fish matches the river's supporting connection.

activities.context: The students arrived at the forest entrance at Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh. Tall trees stood nearby and birds were chirping. Abha Didi, a nature scientist who studies plants and animals, said she would guide them as they explored. One student carried a polythene bag, while another reached towards a bird. Abha Didi stopped them and reminded the group to be careful, not tease animals, and leave plants, flowers and the forest clean.
activities.prompt: Abha Didi notices the polythene bag. What should she do?
options: Tell the student not to carry that bag while visiting the forest.
Say the bag is allowed because the student might need it.
Ask the student to use the bag to pick forest flowers.
Tell the student to put forest garbage in the bag.

why.Say the bag is allowed because the stude: Mistake: this allows an item that is not permitted.
why.Ask the student to use the bag to pick f: Mistake: picking flowers would damage the plants.
why.Tell the student to put forest garbage i: Mistake: forest garbage must not be collected or thrown there.

activities.explanation: Correct: polythene bags should not be brought into the forest.

activities.context: The students arrived at the forest entrance at Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh. Tall trees stood nearby and birds were chirping. Abha Didi, a nature scientist who studies plants and animals, said she would guide them as they explored. One student carried a polythene bag, while another reached towards a bird. Abha Didi stopped them and reminded the group to be careful, not tease animals, and leave plants, flowers and the forest clean.
activities.prompt: While exploring, a student sees a flower and wants to pull it. What should the student do?
options: Leave the flower on the plant and continue exploring without taking it.
Pull the flower and give it to another student.
Break a nearby branch so the group can see where it grows.
Pick the flower and carry it back with the group.

why.Pull the flower and give it to another s: Mistake: pulling the flower damages it.
why.Break a nearby branch so the group can s: Mistake: breaking a branch damages a tree.
why.Pick the flower and carry it back with t: Mistake: taking the flower also damages the plant.

activities.explanation: Correct: plants and flowers must not be damaged.

activities.prompt: Why should visitors follow Abha Didi's instructions while exploring the forest?
activities.answer: Abha Didi studies plants and animals and will guide the students as they explore the forest. Following her instructions helps the students be careful, avoid harming living things, and follow the safety rules for the nature trail.
points: Abha Didi is a nature scientist.
She studies plants and animals.
She will guide the students.
Her instructions promote care and safety.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The students travelled to the forest in jeeps and saw many different plants and animals. Near the pond, they found footprints in the mud, while a rabbit was munching grass close by. They also saw a hornbill with a long tail, a large curved beak, and headgear growing from its forehead like a horn. During the trip, an elephant used its long trunk to take food and water, and a sparrow cracked seeds with its short, strong beak.
activities.prompt: The students want to investigate the footprints without making them disappear. What should they do first?
options: Observe them from nearby without stepping into the prints.
Step through the prints to make clearer examples.
Follow the prints at once and try to catch the animal.
Move the rabbit beside the prints to test whether it made them.

why.Step through the prints to make clearer: Stepping in them would spoil their shape.
why.Follow the prints at once and try to cat: Following them could disturb the animal and the area.
why.Move the rabbit beside the prints to tes: Moving the rabbit would not prove who made the original prints.

activities.explanation: Watching from nearby protects the evidence.

activities.context: The students travelled to the forest in jeeps and saw many different plants and animals. Near the pond, they found footprints in the mud, while a rabbit was munching grass close by. They also saw a hornbill with a long tail, a large curved beak, and headgear growing from its forehead like a horn. During the trip, an elephant used its long trunk to take food and water, and a sparrow cracked seeds with its short, strong beak.
activities.prompt: Why was the sparrow able to open the seeds?
options: The short, powerful bill was able to split the seed shell.
The long trunk was able to pull seeds from plants.
The big, curved bill was able to crush the seeds.
The forehead horn could strike the seeds open.

why.The long trunk was able to pull seeds fr: A trunk is the elephant’s feeding tool.
why.The big, curved bill was able to crush t: The big, curved bill belonged to the hornbill.
why.The forehead horn could strike the seeds: The case does not say that headgear cracks seeds.

activities.explanation: The sparrow’s short, strong beak was used for cracking seeds.

activities.prompt: How does an elephant get food and water differently from a sparrow getting seeds?
activities.answer: An elephant uses its long trunk to take food and water. A sparrow has a short, strong beak, which it uses for cracking seeds. The elephant’s trunk and the sparrow’s strong beak are therefore different tools for getting food.
points: The elephant uses its long trunk.
The trunk helps the elephant take food and water.
The sparrow has a short, strong beak.
The strong beak is used for cracking seeds.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student watches an eagle. Its sharp, curved beak and sharp claws help it catch prey. Later, the student sees a sunbird at flowers and notices its long beak, which helps it drink nectar. The student closes their eyes and listens to different bird sounds. They then open their eyes, focus on one bird at a time, and watch how it moves, eats, and sits. Finally, they write their observations in a bird diary.
activities.prompt: Why are the eagle's curved beak and sharp claws useful for catching prey?
options: Because the eagle uses both the beak and the claws to help catch its food.
Because the curved beak helps it drink nectar and the claws help it catch prey.
Because the long beak helps it catch prey and the curved beak helps it drink nectar.
Because the curved beak helps it catch prey and the claws help it drink nectar.

why.Because the curved beak helps it drink n: The beak's function is confused with the sunbird's nectar drinking.
why.Because the long beak helps it catch pre: The sunbird's long beak is wrongly linked to catching prey.
why.Because the curved beak helps it catch p: The claws' function is confused with drinking nectar.

activities.explanation: Correct: the beak and claws both help the eagle catch prey.

activities.context: A student watches an eagle. Its sharp, curved beak and sharp claws help it catch prey. Later, the student sees a sunbird at flowers and notices its long beak, which helps it drink nectar. The student closes their eyes and listens to different bird sounds. They then open their eyes, focus on one bird at a time, and watch how it moves, eats, and sits. Finally, they write their observations in a bird diary.
activities.prompt: Which observations best describe what the student watches the chosen bird doing?
options: Its body movements, feeding actions, and sitting position.
The beaks and claws of different birds without watching what a chosen bird does.
The sounds of all the birds without opening the eyes to watch one.
The beak and claws of one bird without noticing how that bird behaves.

why.The beaks and claws of different birds w: Looking at different birds does not describe the chosen bird's actions.
why.The sounds of all the birds without open: Listening to birds does not show what the chosen bird is doing.
why.The beak and claws of one bird without n: A beak and claws are features, but they do not describe the bird's actions.

activities.explanation: Correct: movement, eating, and sitting are all observed behaviors.

activities.prompt: Explain why the eagle and the sunbird have different beaks.
activities.answer: An eagle's beak is sharp and curved, and its claws are sharp, so both help it catch prey. A sunbird has a long beak instead, which helps it drink nectar from flowers. The beaks are different because the birds have different eating habits.
points: The eagle has a sharp, curved beak.
The eagle's beak and claws help it catch prey.
The sunbird has a long beak for drinking nectar.
Different eating habits need different beak features.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a place with water animals, a fish uses its fins to swim. A gharial has a long, narrow and pointed snout. A turtle's strong shell keeps it safe, and its webbed feet help it swim easily. A frog can live both on land and in water. In a forest, a grasshopper has three pairs of legs, one pair of antennae to sense its surroundings, and sometimes two pairs of wings. The forest has a wonderful diversity of animals.
activities.prompt: If the turtle's shell became weak, what would the learner expect?
options: It might be less safe.
It might lose its webbed feet.
It might be unable to sense its surroundings.
It might be unable to swim with its fins.

Webbed feet are a separate turtle feature.
why.It might be unable to sense its surround: Sensing surroundings is linked to antennae, not the shell.
why.It might be unable to swim with its fins: Fins belong to fish, not turtles.

activities.explanation: The strong shell keeps the turtle safe.

activities.context: At a place with water animals, a fish uses its fins to swim. A gharial has a long, narrow and pointed snout. A turtle's strong shell keeps it safe, and its webbed feet help it swim easily. A frog can live both on land and in water. In a forest, a grasshopper has three pairs of legs, one pair of antennae to sense its surroundings, and sometimes two pairs of wings. The forest has a wonderful diversity of animals.
activities.prompt: If the grasshopper's antennae could no longer sense its surroundings, what might happen?
options: It might notice its surroundings less well.
It might become less safe because its shell is weak.
It might have more difficulty swimming.
It might have a shorter and less pointed snout.

why.It might become less safe because its sh: The shell, not the antennae, keeps the turtle safe.
Webbed feet and fins help animals swim.
why.It might have a shorter and less pointed: A gharial has the long, narrow and pointed snout.

activities.explanation: The antennae help the insect sense its surroundings.

activities.context: At a place with water animals, a fish uses its fins to swim. A gharial has a long, narrow and pointed snout. A turtle's strong shell keeps it safe, and its webbed feet help it swim easily. A frog can live both on land and in water. In a forest, a grasshopper has three pairs of legs, one pair of antennae to sense its surroundings, and sometimes two pairs of wings. The forest has a wonderful diversity of animals.
activities.prompt: If the fish's fins stopped helping it swim, what might happen?
options: It might have more difficulty swimming.
It might become less safe.
It might sense its surroundings less well.
It might be less able to live both on land and in water.

The strong shell keeps the turtle safe.
why.It might sense its surroundings less wel: Antennae help insects sense their surroundings.
why.It might be less able to live both on la: Frogs can live both on land and in water.

activities.explanation: The fish uses its fins to help it swim.

activities.prompt: Explain how the turtle's shell and webbed feet help it in different ways.
activities.answer: A turtle's strong shell keeps it safe. Its webbed feet help it swim easily. The shell gives protection, while the webbed feet help the turtle move through water easily.
points: The shell is strong.
The shell keeps the turtle safe.
The webbed feet help it swim easily.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a neighbourhood walk, some students collected leaves from different plants. They observed the leaves’ colours, textures, shapes, and vein patterns. One student wanted to make a leaf autograph. The student placed a leaf with its rough, vein-side facing up, covered it with plain paper, and rubbed a crayon over the paper. The students then tried to name the plant or tree each leaf belonged to.
activities.prompt: What happens when the student rubs a crayon over the paper covering the leaf?
options: The leaf’s shape appears on the paper.
The paper hides the leaf’s vein pattern.
The leaf’s colours are painted onto the paper.
The leaf’s vein pattern disappears from the paper.

The paper is used to reveal the pattern, not hide it.
why.The leaf’s colours are painted onto the: The rubbing shows the leaf’s shape and pattern.
why.The leaf’s vein pattern disappears from: The purpose is to make the pattern visible.

activities.explanation: This is what the crayon rubbing is meant to show.

activities.context: During a neighbourhood walk, some students collected leaves from different plants. They observed the leaves’ colours, textures, shapes, and vein patterns. One student wanted to make a leaf autograph. The student placed a leaf with its rough, vein-side facing up, covered it with plain paper, and rubbed a crayon over the paper. The students then tried to name the plant or tree each leaf belonged to.
activities.prompt: Why should the rough, vein-side of the leaf face upwards during a leaf autograph?
options: So that the crayon can show the leaf’s shape and vein pattern.
So that the leaf will look smooth.
So that the veins will be hidden from the crayon.
So that the paper will not touch the leaf.

The rough side is used to show details, not hide them.
why.So that the veins will be hidden from th: The veins should help create the visible pattern.
why.So that the paper will not touch the lea: The paper must cover the leaf.

activities.explanation: The rough side helps reveal the leaf’s pattern.

activities.prompt: How can pictures of leaves help us identify a plant?
activities.answer: Plants can be identified by comparing pictures of their leaves with leaves we observe. A leaf may have a colour, texture, shape, and vein arrangement. Looking at these features helps us identify the plant or tree from which the leaf came.
points: Compare observed leaves with pictures of leaves.
Notice colour, texture, and shape.
Look at the vein arrangement.
Use the leaf to identify its plant or tree.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a nature activity, each child receives a card naming a plant, animal, or natural element. One child holds the yarn and thinks of a connection with another child. The yarn is passed to the player whose card matches that connection. A tree provides food for a bird, and a river supports a fish. After several connections, the children notice that the growing web shows how losing one part can weaken the whole web.
activities.prompt: The player holding the yarn has a tree card and thinks of the connection between a tree and a bird. What should happen next?
options: The yarn should be passed to the player holding the bird card.
The yarn should be passed to the player holding the river card because it is also a natural element.
The player should keep holding the yarn because the connection does not need to match another card.
The yarn should be passed to whichever player is nearest, regardless of that player's card.

why.The yarn should be passed to the player: A river supports a fish, so the river card does not match this connection.
why.The player should keep holding the yarn: The yarn must go to the player with the matching connection.
why.The yarn should be passed to whichever p: Distance from the yarn holder does not determine who receives it.

activities.explanation: The bird card matches the tree-and-bird connection.

activities.context: During a nature activity, each child receives a card naming a plant, animal, or natural element. One child holds the yarn and thinks of a connection with another child. The yarn is passed to the player whose card matches that connection. A tree provides food for a bird, and a river supports a fish. After several connections, the children notice that the growing web shows how losing one part can weaken the whole web.
activities.prompt: If the tree disappears from the nature activity, what is the most likely effect on the web?
options: The tree-and-bird connection would be lost, and the web would become weaker.
The web would stay just as strong because the other yarn connections are still present.
The whole web would collapse because the tree supports every other connection.
Only the bird's card would disappear, while the web would stay unchanged.

why.The web would stay just as strong becaus: Other connections do not prevent a missing part from weakening the web.
why.The whole web would collapse because the: The tree does not support every connection in the web.
why.Only the bird's card would disappear, wh: Losing a part affects the web and cannot be treated as no change.

activities.explanation: Removing the tree removes an important connection in the web.

activities.title: Bird Watching

where plants are collected
when animals grow old

sparrow
grasshopper
gharial

activities.title: Nature Connections

activities.title: When Part Disappears
activities.prompt: One part of the nature web disappears. What can happen?

chapters.title: Growing up with Nature
chapters.summary: In this chapter: journey to the solar-powered village; art and natural dyes; farming, honey and natural helpers; celebrations, sacred groves and local rituals.

lessons.title: Journey to the Solar-Powered Village

activities.prompt: What might make a village shine while a forest glows like flames?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Special Family Visit
activities.body: Reena and Amit are going to their village near a forest. The visit happens during the harvest festival. The village will become fully powered by solar energy. They cannot wait to see it shining for the celebrations. Bright orange-red Palash flowers can make the forest look reddish-orange. The houses use natural materials, and Reena’s grandmother painted a wall.
keyPoints: The family visit happens during the harvest festival.
Solar energy will fully power the village.
Palash flowers make the forest look reddish-orange.
activities.explanation: This journey brings together a festival, solar energy, colourful trees, and family creativity.

activities.prompt: Reena and Amit visit their forest-side village during a harvest festival. Why might they expect bright lights?
steps: The visit happens during a harvest festival, so celebrations matter.
The village will become fully powered by solar energy.
Solar energy can make the village shine during the celebrations.
Therefore, Reena and Amit expect to see the village shining.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Colourful Trees and Village Art
activities.body: Reena and Amit notice trees covered with bright orange-red flowers. These Palash flowers can make the whole forest look reddish-orange. Palash is also called the flame of forest. In the village, houses are made with natural materials. One wall has a painting made by Reena’s grandmother. She made a dye by mixing rice flour and water.
keyPoints: Palash flowers can make the forest look reddish-orange.
Village houses use natural materials.
Reena’s grandmother made a dye with rice flour and water.
activities.explanation: The village shows nature’s beauty through its flowers, houses, and colourful wall art.

activities.prompt: What was happening when Reena and Amit visited the village?
options: A harvest festival
A house-building lesson
A solar-panel workshop
A tree-planting event
activities.explanation: Good choice! The family visit happened during the harvest festival.

activities.prompt: The Palash tree is also called the flame of the sea.
activities.explanation: You remembered the special name! Palash is called the flame of forest.

activities.prompt: The flowering tree is called a ______ tree.
activities.hint: It is known as the flame of forest.
activities.explanation: Well done! Palash is the tree covered with bright orange-red flowers.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each detail connects closely with the right part of the story.

activities.prompt: What makes the whole forest look reddish-orange?
options: Palash flowers
Rice-water dye
Wall paint
Solar panels
activities.explanation: Excellent! The blooming Palash flowers can colour the whole forest reddish-orange.

activities.prompt: The village houses were made with natural materials.
activities.explanation: Correct! The village houses were built using natural materials.

activities.prompt: Reena and Amit see bright orange-red flowers on trees near their village. Why is Palash called the flame of forest?
options: Its orange-red bloom can make the forest look pale and gray.
Its orange-red bloom can make the forest look reddish-orange.
Its orange-red bloom can make the forest look dark and empty.
Its orange-red bloom can make the village houses shine at night.

why.Its orange-red bloom can make the forest: This wrongly changes the bright bloom into a pale, gray forest.
This wrongly changes the bright bloom into a dark, empty forest.
why.Its orange-red bloom can make the villag: This puts the forest's color effect onto the village houses.

activities.explanation: The orange-red bloom can make the forest look reddish-orange.

activities.prompt: Village houses are made with natural materials. A child wants to test a model house. Which check is fairest?
options: Check whether its walls have bright flowers.
Check whether it shines during the festival.
Check whether its materials come from nature.
Check whether a grandmother painted its walls.

why.Check whether its walls have bright flow: This checks wall flowers instead of the house materials.
why.Check whether it shines during the festi: This checks festival light instead of the house materials.
why.Check whether a grandmother painted its: This checks the painter instead of the house materials.

activities.explanation: Natural materials are the village house feature being checked.

activities.prompt: Reena sees a wall painting made by her grandmother. The grandmother used rice flour and water for her dye. Why is a flour-only claim flawed?
options: Both rice flour and water must be mixed together.
Only rice flour should be mixed, but water should not.
Only water should be mixed, but rice flour should not.
Rice flour and water should be kept in separate bowls.

why.Only rice flour should be mixed, but wat: This wrongly leaves water out of the mixing method.
why.Only water should be mixed, but rice flo: This wrongly leaves rice flour out of the mixing method.
why.Rice flour and water should be kept in s: This wrongly keeps the two ingredients apart.

activities.explanation: The method says to mix rice flour and water together.

activities.prompt: Bright orange-red flowers bloom on Palash trees. Why is the claim that every forest must look reddish-orange too strong?
options: The flowers will always make the forest look exactly reddish-orange.
The flowers can make only the village houses look reddish-orange.
The flowers could make the forest look reddish-orange, not must.
The flowers can affect only one tree, not the whole forest.

why.The flowers will always make the forest: This wrongly turns a possible effect into an always, exact result.
why.The flowers can make only the village ho: This wrongly puts the forest's color effect onto village houses.
why.The flowers can affect only one tree, no: This wrongly assumes one blooming tree cannot affect the whole forest.

activities.explanation: The bloom could make the forest reddish-orange, but need not.

lessons.title: Art and Natural Dyes

activities.prompt: Could flowers and leaves turn into colourful paint for cloth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Colours from nature
activities.body: Natural dyes come from flowers, leaves, barks and roots. Beetroot, hibiscus and marigold had colouring properties. This means they could give colour. Makers boil collected plant parts in water, then strain the liquid. The dye can paint a light-coloured handkerchief. The cloth must soak overnight and dry the next morning. Paint can also use powdered coloured stones. Gond art paints nature on walls with natural colours.
keyPoints: Plant parts can provide natural dye.
Straining removes plant materials from the liquid.
Gond art uses natural colours on walls.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how plants and stones can make colours.

activities.prompt: Reena wants to dye a light-coloured handkerchief with hibiscus flowers. What should she do?
steps: Boil the flowers in water because this releases their colour.
Strain the liquid because the dye stays after plant materials are removed.
Paint the light-coloured cloth because the dye can colour it.
Soak overnight and dry next morning, so the cloth is dyed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A painting scene
activities.prompt: Who did Reena and Amit see painting on a cloth?
options: Their grandmother
Reena
Amit
Their teacher
activities.explanation: Reena and Amit saw their grandmother painting on a cloth.

activities.title: Gond art
activities.prompt: Gond art used natural colours to paint pictures on walls.
activities.explanation: Gond art was painting on walls using natural colours.

activities.title: Making natural dye
activities.prompt: Put the steps for making and using natural dye in order.
items: Leave natural dye after removing plant materials
activities.explanation: Boiling, straining and removing the plant materials left the natural dye.

activities.title: Removing plant materials
activities.prompt: After boiling, the liquid was ______ so plant materials could be removed.
activities.hint: Remove the plant materials from the liquid.
activities.explanation: Straining removed the plant materials from the liquid.

activities.title: Why strain the liquid?
activities.prompt: Why was the liquid strained?
options: To remove plant materials
To add coloured stones
To dry the cloth
To make wall pictures
activities.explanation: The liquid was strained so plant materials could be removed.

activities.title: Drying the cloth
activities.prompt: The cloth was dried immediately after the plant materials were strained.
activities.explanation: The cloth was soaked overnight and dried the next morning.

activities.title: Plants with colouring properties
activities.prompt: Which group is named as having colouring properties?
options: Beetroot, hibiscus and marigold
Trees, animals and humans
Cloth, water and paint
Stones, birds and leaves
activities.explanation: Beetroot, hibiscus and marigold had colouring properties.

activities.prompt: A child boils beetroot in water, and the water becomes coloured. What happens next?
options: The plant materials are strained out.
The plant materials are boiled again.
The dye is strained out too.
The water is left unboiled.

This repeats boiling instead of removing the solid plant materials.
This confuses the dye with the plant materials that should be removed.
The collected plant parts were boiled before the liquid was strained.

activities.explanation: Straining removes plant materials while the dye stays in the liquid.

activities.prompt: A child compares overnight soaking with a quick dip using natural dye. Which test is fair?
options: Use two cloths, same dye, different soaking times.
Use two cloths, different dyes, same soaking time.
Use one cloth, different dyes, different soaking times.
Use one cloth, same dye, different drying times.

why.Use two cloths, different dyes, same soa: Both dye and soaking time change, so the test has two changes.
why.Use one cloth, different dyes, different: One cloth cannot compare two soaking times, and dye also changes.
why.Use one cloth, same dye, different dryin: This changes drying time instead of comparing overnight soaking with a dip.

activities.explanation: Only soaking time changes, so the two cloths can be compared fairly.
