activities.explanation: The paper boats did different things in the rain puddle.

activities.title: Test at Home
activities.prompt: A paper boat can be floated in a ______ at home.
activities.hint: Choose the container you can use at home.
activities.explanation: A bowl lets you float a paper boat at home.

activities.title: Match the Objects
activities.prompt: Match each object with the correct result or detail.
activities.explanation: Leaves float, iron nails sink, and the other pairs show test containers.

activities.title: What Should You Do First?
activities.prompt: What should you do before dropping each object into water?
options: Measure
Count
Guess
Write
activities.explanation: The lesson asks children to make a guess before each object enters water.

activities.title: Heavy Iron Nails
activities.prompt: Heavy iron nails float in water.
activities.explanation: Heavy iron nails sink, while lighter leaves float.

activities.title: Choose the Record
activities.prompt: Which pair records an object that sinks?
options: F and float
F and sink
S and sink
S and float
activities.explanation: F means float and S means sink, so this pair records sinking.

activities.title: Test an Object
activities.prompt: Put the testing steps in the correct order.
items: Check whether it floats or sinks
Show the result with F or S
activities.explanation: Guessing comes first, then dropping and checking. The letter marks the result.

activities.prompt: A child says, "Every light object floats because weight decides everything." Why is this claim flawed?
options: Other factors also affect whether objects float or sink.
Heavy objects always sink, so weight decides everything.
Light objects always float, so weight decides everything.
Only iron nails can sink in a bucket of water.

why.Heavy objects always sink, so weight dec: This still assumes weight alone controls every result.
why.Light objects always float, so weight de: This also assumes weight alone controls every result.
why.Only iron nails can sink in a bucket of: This wrongly limits sinking to one type of object.

activities.explanation: This rejects the idea that weight alone decides the result.

lessons.title: Changing Shapes and Making Boats

activities.prompt: What could we discover by changing the same piece of foil?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Change, Compare and Improve
activities.body: Try changing the shape of a floating object. Aluminium foil can float when spread out or shaped like a cup. It sinks when pressed tightly into a ball. Next, make a boat from materials such as paper, cardboard, sticks, clay and tape. Compare each boat with the other boats, then improve the designs.
keyPoints: Shape can change floating and sinking.
Spread-out and cup-like foil floated; a tight ball sank.
Boats are made, compared and improved.
activities.explanation: You can test the shape, then compare the boats.

activities.title: Change the shape, not the weight

tasks.then: Spread out or made into a cup, the foil pushes aside enough water to hold it up.
A cup traps air and pushes aside more water than the foil weighs, so it floats.

activities.takeaway: Floating depends on how much water a shape pushes aside, not just on its weight: a tight ball of foil sinks, but the same foil spread out flat or shaped into a cup floats.
activities.explanation: Floating depends on how much water a shape pushes aside, not just on its weight: a tight ball of foil sinks, but the same foil spread out flat or shaped into a cup floats.

activities.prompt: A child wants aluminium foil to float. What should the child do with its shape?
steps: Spread the foil out because spread-out foil floated.
Make it cup-like because a foil cup also floated.
Do not press it into a ball because the ball sank.
Choose a spread or cup shape because shape can change floating.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which foil shape sank?
options: Tight foil ball
Spread-out foil
Foil cup shape
activities.explanation: The foil sank when pressed tightly into a ball. Shape can change whether something floats or sinks.

activities.prompt: Aluminium foil floated when it was spread out.
activities.explanation: The foil floated when spread out. Trying different shapes is a useful test.

activities.prompt: Boats can be made from paper, ______, sticks, clay and tape.
activities.hint: Another boat-making material.
activities.explanation: Cardboard is one of the materials children can use to make boats.

activities.prompt: Match each material to the boat it can make.
activities.explanation: Paper, cardboard, sticks and clay can all be used to make boats.

activities.prompt: Put these actions in order.
items: Compare it with the other boats
activities.explanation: First make the boat, then compare it, and finally improve its design.

activities.prompt: Boat designs cannot be improved after the boats are compared.
activities.explanation: Boat designs can be improved after the comparison. Use what you learn to improve the next design.

activities.prompt: One foil test spreads foil. Another presses foil tightly into a ball. Which test fairly checks shape?
options: Use the same foil. Spread it, then make it into a ball.
Use different foil. Spread a piece, then press another piece.
Add more foil, then press all of it into a ball.
Use the same foil, but change its amount and shape each time.

why.Use different foil. Spread a piece, then: Different foil makes the comparison less fair.
why.Add more foil, then press all of it into: Adding foil changes the amount of foil as well.
why.Use the same foil, but change its amount: Changing both amount and shape does not test shape alone.

activities.explanation: Only the foil's shape changes between the two tests.

activities.prompt: The class has paper, cardboard, sticks, clay and tape. It organises a boat exhibition. What should the class do next?
options: Make boats, compare them, and improve their designs.
Make cups, compare them, and improve their designs.
Make boats, compare them, and keep every design.
Make boats, skip comparisons, and improve every design.

why.Make cups, compare them, and improve the: This child focuses on cups instead of the planned boats.
why.Make boats, compare them, and keep every: This child misses that designs can improve after comparison.
why.Make boats, skip comparisons, and improv: This child thinks improvement can happen without comparing boats.

activities.explanation: These materials make boats, and comparison can guide design improvements.

activities.prompt: Children make boats in groups of three or four. Which group size is not allowed?
options: A group with only two children.
A group with exactly three children.
A group with exactly four children.
A group with three or four children.

Three children fit the group rule.
Four children fit the group rule.
Both three and four are allowed.

activities.explanation: Two children are not in a group of three or four.

activities.context: Every day, Meera and Dhruv see and use things around them, and some of these things help them work. Meera uses a pencil for writing, while a bag carries books. Every weekend, they discover something new to explore. Meera spun a coin and watched it closely. As the coin slowed down, it began to shake, and she wondered why. She also wanted to know how a top spins.
activities.prompt: If Meera replaced the coin with an eraser and tried the same activity, what should she expect?
options: It will not spin properly.
It will spin smoothly like a coin and a bangle.
It will begin to shake as it slows down.
It will carry books while turning around.

why.It will spin smoothly like a coin and a: This wrongly treats an eraser like a coin or bangle.
The shaking movement is described for the coin, not the eraser.
why.It will carry books while turning around: This wrongly gives the eraser the bag's job.

activities.explanation: Correct: erasers do not spin properly.

activities.context: Every day, Meera and Dhruv see and use things around them, and some of these things help them work. Meera uses a pencil for writing, while a bag carries books. Every weekend, they discover something new to explore. Meera spun a coin and watched it closely. As the coin slowed down, it began to shake, and she wondered why. She also wanted to know how a top spins.
activities.prompt: Which activity would best help Meera find out how a top spins?
options: Spin the top and observe how it moves.
Write with the top and judge its movement.
Carry books with the top and watch the books.
Compare the top with an eraser without spinning either.

why.Write with the top and judge its movemen: This wrongly treats the top like a pencil.
why.Carry books with the top and watch the b: This wrongly treats the top like a bag.
why.Compare the top with an eraser without s: This does not show how the top moves.

activities.explanation: Correct: direct observation can show how a top spins.

activities.prompt: How does spinning compare with what an eraser does?
activities.answer: Coins and bangles can spin, but erasers do not spin properly. A spinning coin begins to shake as it slows down. Meera and Dhruv can compare these movements and explore how spinning works and why the coin's movement was different from an eraser's.
points: Coins and bangles can spin.
Erasers do not spin properly.
A coin begins to shake as it slows down.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child makes two spinners from cardboard, toothpicks and small objects. One has a toothpick at its centre. The other has a toothpick away from its centre. The child spins both and records what happens. The first spinner looks the same from all sides and stays upright while it spins. The second spinner does not behave in the same way. The child changes the toothpick length below the cardboard and the cardboard's alignment to help a spinner spin better.
activities.prompt: A spinner is not working properly. What should the child do to try to improve it?
options: Adjust how far the toothpick extends under the card, then realign the card.
Replace the cardboard with an empty ballpoint pen tube.
Keep the toothpick and cardboard exactly as they are and stop testing.
Move the toothpick away from the middle of the cardboard.

why.Replace the cardboard with an empty ball: The ballpoint pen tube can make a spinner, but it is not the stated way to improve this one.
why.Keep the toothpick and cardboard exactly: Some spinners might not work properly, so stopping the test would not help.
why.Move the toothpick away from the middle: Moving the toothpick away from the centre is not given as a way to improve the spin.

activities.explanation: Changing the toothpick length and cardboard alignment can help a spinner spin better.

activities.context: A child makes two spinners from cardboard, toothpicks and small objects. One has a toothpick at its centre. The other has a toothpick away from its centre. The child spins both and records what happens. The first spinner looks the same from all sides and stays upright while it spins. The second spinner does not behave in the same way. The child changes the toothpick length below the cardboard and the cardboard's alignment to help a spinner spin better.
activities.prompt: After changing the toothpick length below the cardboard and the cardboard's alignment, what can the child expect?
options: The spinner's spinning may improve.
The spinner will certainly work properly on the next spin.
The spinner will look the same from every side.
The spinner will remain upright throughout the spin.

why.The spinner will certainly work properly: The changes do not guarantee that the spinner will work properly.
why.The spinner will look the same from ever: Changing the length and alignment is linked to better spinning, not to one appearance from every side.
why.The spinner will remain upright througho: Upright movement was described for the first spinner, not promised for every changed spinner.

activities.explanation: These changes can help a spinner spin better, so improvement is possible.

activities.prompt: Explain how a child can test and improve a spinner.
activities.answer: The child should spin each spinner and record what happens. If it does not work properly, the child can change the length of the toothpick below the cardboard or change the cardboard's alignment. Spinning and recording again after a change can show whether the spinner now spins better.
points: Spins the spinner and records observations.
Changes the toothpick length below the cardboard and/or the cardboard's alignment.
Tests the spinner again after a change.
Checks whether the spinner now spins better.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child made a spinner from a square card and coloured it in different ways. The child turned the card and noticed that the square looked like a circle while it was moving. Later, the child used a charkha, turning its large wheel by hand while it twisted cotton fibre into thread. The child also learned that Mahatma Gandhi used the charkha to make handmade clothes.
activities.prompt: Why did the square card look like a circle?
options: The card's spinning motion made its square shape look circular.
The card's different colours made its square shape look circular.
The charkha's large wheel changed the card's shape permanently.
The card would look circular only after it stopped spinning.

why.The card's different colours made its sq: Wrong: the colours are observed on the spinner; they do not explain its shape.
why.The charkha's large wheel changed the ca: Wrong: the charkha wheel was separate from the card and did not change it.
why.The card would look circular only after: Wrong: the card appeared circular while spinning, not after it stopped.

activities.explanation: Right: the square card appeared circular while it was spinning.

activities.context: A child made a spinner from a square card and coloured it in different ways. The child turned the card and noticed that the square looked like a circle while it was moving. Later, the child used a charkha, turning its large wheel by hand while it twisted cotton fibre into thread. The child also learned that Mahatma Gandhi used the charkha to make handmade clothes.
activities.prompt: What should the child do to use a charkha to twist cotton fibre into thread?
options: Turn the charkha's large wheel by hand.
Spin a coloured card spinner in place of the charkha.
Spin a clay top in place of the charkha.
Turn a potter's wheel in place of the charkha.

why.Spin a coloured card spinner in place of: Wrong: a card spinner is for observing colours while spinning.
Wrong: clay tops are different objects from a charkha.
why.Turn a potter's wheel in place of the ch: Wrong: a potter's wheel is another spinning object, not a charkha.

activities.explanation: Right: turning the large wheel by hand operates the charkha.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a charkha and a card spinner?
activities.answer: A charkha twists cotton fibre into thread. Its large wheel spins when turned by hand. A card spinner is made from a card piece, can have different shapes and colours, and is spun so children can observe its colours. A square card can look circular while it is spinning.
points: A charkha twists cotton fibre into thread.
Its large wheel spins when turned by hand.
A card spinner can have different shapes and colours.
Children observe a spinning spinner's colours.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Meera and Dhruv saw rain water form a puddle. They placed their paper boats in it. Some boats floated properly, but others flipped. The children checked each result. They also thought about other objects that could be tested, such as leaves, nails, bowls, bottles, stones and foil. For every object, they guessed first. Then they dropped it into a bucket of water and used F or S to record what happened.
activities.prompt: Before testing an object in the bucket, what should the children do?
options: Predict whether it will float or sink.
Drop it into the water without making a guess.
Choose an object only by how heavy it feels.
Record the result before making any guess.

why.Drop it into the water without making a: Skipping the guess removes the prediction step.
why.Choose an object only by how heavy it fe: Weight alone cannot decide the result.
why.Record the result before making any gues: The result is known only after the test.

activities.explanation: Testing should begin with a guess.

activities.context: Meera and Dhruv saw rain water form a puddle. They placed their paper boats in it. Some boats floated properly, but others flipped. The children checked each result. They also thought about other objects that could be tested, such as leaves, nails, bowls, bottles, stones and foil. For every object, they guessed first. Then they dropped it into a bucket of water and used F or S to record what happened.
activities.prompt: Why might some paper boats float properly while others flip in the puddle?
options: Factors besides weight can affect floating and sinking.
The heavier boats must always flip.
The lighter boats must always float properly.
All paper boats must behave in exactly the same way.

Weight alone does not always decide the result.
why.The lighter boats must always float prop: Lighter boats do not always float properly.
why.All paper boats must behave in exactly t: Some boats floated properly while others flipped.

activities.explanation: Other factors affect floating and sinking.

activities.prompt: Why can weight alone not be used to decide whether an object will float or sink?
activities.answer: Leaves and heavy iron nails show that weight alone cannot explain floating and sinking. Lighter leaves float, while heavy iron nails sink. Other factors also affect whether an object floats or sinks, so children should test an object and use F or S instead of deciding from weight by itself.
points: Lighter leaves float.
Heavy iron nails sink.
Weight alone does not decide the result.
Other factors also affect floating and sinking.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a class activity, Ravi's group changed aluminium foil in three ways. They spread it out, pressed it tightly into a ball, and shaped it like a cup. They then made boats from paper, cardboard, sticks, clay and tape. The class organised an exhibition, and each group compared its boat with the others. After the comparison, the group decided which boat design could be improved.
activities.prompt: If the group spreads the aluminium foil out again before the foil test, what would happen next?
options: It would float, because the spread-out shape has already been tested successfully.
It would sink, because the foil becomes heavier when it is spread out.
It would float, because a ball shape can stay on top of the water.
It would sink, because aluminium foil always sinks in every shape.

why.It would sink, because the foil becomes: Spreading it out does not make it heavier.
why.It would float, because a ball shape can: The ball shape was the one that sank.
why.It would sink, because aluminium foil al: The result depends on the shape, not one rule for every shape.

activities.explanation: Spreading the foil out is the shape that floated.

activities.context: During a class activity, Ravi's group changed aluminium foil in three ways. They spread it out, pressed it tightly into a ball, and shaped it like a cup. They then made boats from paper, cardboard, sticks, clay and tape. The class organised an exhibition, and each group compared its boat with the others. After the comparison, the group decided which boat design could be improved.
activities.prompt: After the exhibition, what should Ravi's group do to improve its boat?
options: Use what it learned from comparing the boats to improve its design.
Keep the design unchanged, because an exhibition is only for looking.
Change the material first, because comparing designs cannot improve a boat.
Make every boat in the class identical, because different designs should not be compared.

why.Keep the design unchanged, because an ex: An exhibition allows the boats to be compared.
why.Change the material first, because compa: Changing a material alone is not what the comparison shows.
why.Make every boat in the class identical,: Different designs are compared so groups can consider improvements.

activities.explanation: Boat designs can be improved after a comparison.

activities.prompt: Explain why changing the shape of the aluminium foil changed whether it floated or sank.
activities.answer: Changing the shape of the foil can change whether it floats or sinks. The foil floated when it was spread out or shaped like a cup, but it sank when pressed tightly into a ball. This shows that the foil's shape affects whether it floats or sinks.
points: Changing shape can change floating or sinking.
The spread-out foil floated.
The cup-shaped foil floated.
The ball-shaped foil sank.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

lessons.title: Paper and Trees

activities.prompt: Can trees become paper, and can we make paper again?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Paper Comes from Trees
activities.body: Paper is made from trees. Pihu's drawing book is made from trees too. Recycled paper means paper that is used again. A pot can look like paper, but its surface feels rough. This pot is made from recycled paper. Recycling paper helps us save trees. Pihu sees trees pictured on a newspaper's front page. Pihu asks whether they can make paper like the pot's.
keyPoints: Paper is made from trees.
Recycling paper helps us save trees.
The pot looks like paper but feels rough.
activities.explanation: Paper, trees and recycling are closely connected.

activities.prompt: Can Pihu make paper like the rough pot's paper while helping trees?
steps: The pot looks like paper and feels rough unlike Pihu's drawing book.
It is made from recycled paper, so rough paper can still be paper.
This shows Pihu can ask for paper like the pot's from recycled paper.
Recycling paper helps save trees, so this choice can also help save trees.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Pihu's Drawing Book
activities.prompt: What is Pihu's drawing book made from?
options: Trees
Newspaper
Recycled paper
A rough surface
activities.explanation: Yes! Pihu's drawing book is made from trees.

activities.title: Fill in the Blank
activities.prompt: Pihu's drawing book is made from ______.
activities.hint: Think about what paper is made from.
activities.explanation: Well done! The drawing book is made from trees.

activities.title: Match the Facts
activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
pairs: Can they make paper like the pot's
activities.explanation: Paper and the drawing book come from trees. Pihu asks about making paper like the pot's.

activities.title: Why Recycle Paper?
activities.prompt: Why should we recycle paper?
options: It helps us save the pot.
It makes the pot feel rough.
It helps us save trees.
It puts trees on a page.
activities.explanation: Recycling paper helps us save trees. The pot is also made from recycled paper.

activities.title: From Trees to the Pot
activities.prompt: Put the materials in order from their starting material to the finished pot.
activities.explanation: Paper starts with trees. Recycled paper is then used to make the pot.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Facts
activities.prompt: Which choice uses the lesson's facts correctly?
options: Paper makes trees, and recycling paper saves books.
Recycled paper makes a pot, and recycling paper saves trees.
Trees make paper, and recycling paper saves pots.
Fresh paper makes a pot, and recycling paper saves water.
activities.explanation: The pot is made from recycled paper. Recycling paper helps us save trees.

activities.prompt: The pot feels rough unlike Pihu's drawing book. Which test fairly compares their surfaces?
options: Touch both surfaces and compare how they feel.
Touch only the pot and guess how the book feels.
Look at both surfaces but do not touch them.
Touch only the book and guess how the pot feels.

why.Touch only the pot and guess how the boo: Touching only the pot cannot directly compare it with the book.
why.Look at both surfaces but do not touch t: Looking cannot show how either surface feels.
why.Touch only the book and guess how the po: Touching only the book leaves out the pot's surface.

activities.explanation: Touching both surfaces gives a fair comparison of how they feel.

activities.prompt: Pihu says, 'The pot cannot be paper because it feels rough.' Why is this material claim flawed?
options: The pot is paper, but its surface can feel rough.
Paper from trees must always feel like the book.
Looking like paper proves that the pot feels rough.
The drawing book and pot must feel exactly the same.

why.Paper from trees must always feel like t: This mistake assumes paper from trees must feel like Pihu's drawing book.
why.Looking like paper proves that the pot f: This mistake confuses how the pot looks with how it feels.
why.The drawing book and pot must feel exact: This mistake thinks two different surfaces must feel the same.

activities.explanation: The pot looks like paper and is made from recycled paper, even though it feels rough.

activities.prompt: Pihu saw a picture of trees on the newspaper's front page. What can the picture show?
options: That the page shows trees, not whole real trees.
That a whole tree is hidden inside the page.
That every picture on the page is a tree.
That the trees have been cut from the page.

why.That a whole tree is hidden inside the p: This mistake treats the pictured trees as real trees inside.
why.That every picture on the page is a tree: This mistake thinks every image on the page shows a tree.
why.That the trees have been cut from the pa: This mistake imagines the picture was cut from real trees.

activities.explanation: A picture shows the trees, not whole real trees inside the page.

activities.prompt: Things around us have different materials. Paper is made from trees. Which action can help save trees?
options: Recycle paper instead of always throwing it away.
Throw paper away instead of recycling it always.
Make new paper and never recycle the old paper.
Keep paper rough and never recycle that paper.

why.Throw paper away instead of recycling it: This mistake throws away paper instead of recycling it.
why.Make new paper and never recycle the old: This mistake thinks making new paper avoids using trees.
why.Keep paper rough and never recycle that: This mistake thinks a rough surface changes what recycling does.

activities.explanation: Recycling paper helps us save trees.

lessons.title: Making Recycled Paper

activities.prompt: What if old newspapers could become a brand-new sheet of paper?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How to Make Recycled Paper
activities.body: Making recycled paper starts with collecting old newspapers, fenugreek seeds and water. Tear the newspapers into small pieces and soak them. Add fenugreek seeds and leave the mixture overnight. Blend or mash the soaked paper and seeds. The mixture becomes wet. Spread the paste on a flat base, roll it into thin sheets and let them dry.
keyPoints: Old newspapers, fenugreek seeds and water are needed.
Fenugreek seeds act as a binding material.
The rolled sheets must dry to make recycled paper.
activities.explanation: Follow these steps to turn old newspapers into recycled paper.

activities.prompt: A child wants to make recycled paper from old newspapers. What should the child do?
steps: Tear the old newspapers into small pieces and soak them in water because soaking prepares them for mashing.
Add a small quantity of fenugreek seeds and leave the mixture overnight because the seeds act as a binding material.
Blend or mash the soaked paper and seeds because this makes a wet mixture.
Spread the paste on a flat base, roll it into thin sheets, and let it dry to make recycled paper.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which item helps bind the paper?
options: Fenugreek seeds
Old newspapers
Water
Paper pieces
activities.explanation: Fenugreek seeds act as a binding material.

activities.prompt: Collect old newspapers, ______ seeds and water.
activities.hint: These seeds help bind the paper.
activities.explanation: Fenugreek seeds are collected to help bind the paper.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its part in making recycled paper.
pairs: Mash by hand or with another tool
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a useful result or job in making recycled paper.

activities.prompt: What should you do after soaking the paper?
options: Add fenugreek seeds and leave overnight.
Add more water and leave overnight.
Tear the seeds into small pieces.
Roll the mixture into a sheet.
activities.explanation: Add a small quantity of fenugreek seeds and leave the mixture overnight.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: This order takes you from collecting materials to drying recycled paper.

activities.prompt: What happens after the blended paper is spread on a flat base?
options: It is rolled into thin sheets.
It is left to dry at once.
It is soaked in water again.
It is torn into small pieces.
activities.explanation: Spread the paste on a flat base and roll it into thin sheets.

activities.prompt: A child makes recycled paper but forgets the fenugreek seeds. What may happen to the sheets?
options: The sheets may not hold together well.
The sheets may become thinner than before.
The mixture may become less wet than before.
The sheets may dry without any rolling.

why.The sheets may become thinner than befor: This mistakes rolling thin for binding the paper sheets.
why.The mixture may become less wet than bef: This mistakes the seeds for the water in the mixture.
This thinks drying can happen before the rolling step.

activities.explanation: Fenugreek seeds act as a binding material, so the sheets may not hold together well.

activities.prompt: A child tears newspaper into small pieces and adds water and fenugreek seeds. Why is the mixture left overnight?
options: So the seeds can help bind the paper mixture.
So the paper pieces become larger sheets.
So the paste can dry before it is rolled.
So the water can make the thin paper sheets.

why.So the paper pieces become larger sheets: This confuses soaking the paper with rolling the paste into sheets.
why.So the paste can dry before it is rolled: This thinks soaking dries the paste before rolling.
why.So the water can make the thin paper she: This thinks water alone makes thin sheets and misses the seeds.

activities.explanation: The seeds act as a binding material in the mixture left overnight.

activities.prompt: Two paper mixtures use the same newspaper and water. One adds fenugreek seeds. Which test is fair?
options: Compare how well each mixture binds into sheets.
Compare which mixture makes larger seeds.
Compare which mixture dries before it is rolled.
Compare which mixture has more newspaper pieces.

why.Compare which mixture makes larger seeds: This mistakes seed size for the binding action.
why.Compare which mixture dries before it is: This focuses on drying instead of checking the sheets.
why.Compare which mixture has more newspaper: This changes the newspaper amount instead of testing the seeds.

activities.explanation: This test checks how the binding material helps the paper form sheets.

activities.prompt: A child says, “I can skip soaking and roll whole newspapers into paper.” What is the flaw?
options: The paper must be torn and soaked first.
The paper must be dried before it is rolled.
The seeds must be rolled instead of mixed.
The base must be made from the seeds.

why.The paper must be dried before it is rol: This puts the final drying step before forming the sheets.
why.The seeds must be rolled instead of mixe: This mistakes the seeds for the paper mixture that is rolled.
This mistakes the seeds for the flat base used for spreading.

activities.explanation: The newspapers must be torn into small pieces and soaked before mashing.

lessons.title: Colouring Recycled Paper

activities.prompt: What colours can we make with plants and paint our recycled paper?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Colours from Nature
activities.body: Paper can use natural or artificial dyes. Natural dyes come from plant parts: leaves, flowers, roots, seeds and stems. They are safe to use. They can colour clothes and pots. You can colour and design recycled paper you have made. Cut it into pieces of the same size. Use the same quantity of ingredient for each piece. You can use other natural ingredients too. Write your observations in the table.
keyPoints: Natural dyes come from plant parts.
Natural dyes are safe to use.
Recycled paper can be coloured and designed.
activities.explanation: Natural dyes use plant parts to colour recycled paper.

activities.prompt: How can we colour equal-sized recycled paper pieces fairly and record what we see?
steps: Cut equal-sized recycled paper pieces, because equal sizes make a fair test.
Use natural table ingredients, because they can colour recycled paper.
Use equal ingredient amounts, because this makes the colouring fair.
Record observations in the table, so our fair test shows what happened.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the Plant-Made Dye
activities.prompt: Which one is made from different parts of plants?
options: Recycled paper
Natural dye
Paper piece
Artificial dye
activities.explanation: The lesson says natural dyes are made from different plant parts.

activities.title: Prepare the Paper
activities.prompt: Cut the recycled paper into pieces of the same ______.
activities.hint: All the pieces should match.
activities.explanation: The lesson asks you to cut the recycled paper into equal-sized pieces.

activities.title: Match Plant Parts
activities.prompt: Match each plant part to the dye it can produce.
activities.explanation: Leaves, flowers, roots, seeds and stems can all provide natural dyes.

activities.title: Use Equal Amounts
activities.prompt: What should you do when colouring each piece?
options: Use equal amounts
Use unequal amounts
Use no ingredients
Use extra ingredients
activities.explanation: The lesson says to use the same quantity of ingredient for each piece.

activities.title: Order the Steps
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Cut the recycled paper into pieces of the same size.
Colour the pieces using natural ingredients from the table.
Write down your observations in the table.
activities.explanation: First cut the paper, then colour the pieces and record your observations.

activities.title: Record Your Work
activities.prompt: What should you write in the table after colouring?
options: More paper pieces
Longer plant parts
Your observations
Different quantities
activities.explanation: Writing down your observations helps you record what happened during colouring.

activities.prompt: Paper is cut into same-sized pieces. Which colouring plan is fairest?
options: Use natural ingredients from the table in equal amounts.
Use natural ingredients from the table in different amounts.
Use natural ingredients on only some paper pieces.
Leave some paper pieces without any colour.

why.Use natural ingredients from the table i: Different amounts confuse equal colouring with uneven colouring.
why.Use natural ingredients on only some pap: This mistakes colouring only some pieces for a complete fair test.
why.Leave some paper pieces without any colo: Leaving pieces out mistakes a colour test for an empty-piece check.

activities.explanation: Equal amounts make the colouring fair and follow the rule.

activities.prompt: Natural dye comes from plant parts. Is it safe to use this dye on a pot?
options: Yes, this natural dye is safe to use.
No, this natural dye is never safe to use.
No, this natural dye can only colour clothes.
Yes, but only artificial dye can colour pots.

why.No, this natural dye is never safe to us: This reverses the safety fact about these natural dyes.
why.No, this natural dye can only colour clo: This confuses dye sources with the things natural dye can colour.
why.Yes, but only artificial dye can colour: This confuses natural dye with artificial dye for colouring pots.

activities.explanation: Natural dyes made this way are safe and can colour pots.

activities.prompt: The paper pieces are the same size. How should we test natural ingredients fairly?
options: Give each ingredient its own piece, using equal amounts.
Mix all the ingredients together on one paper piece.
Give every piece the same first ingredient.
Use more of the ingredient that looks nicer.

why.Mix all the ingredients together on one: Mixing them together hides what each ingredient does alone.
why.Give every piece the same first ingredie: Using one ingredient only does not test the other ingredients.
why.Use more of the ingredient that looks ni: Choosing amounts by looks makes the test unfair.

activities.explanation: Equal amounts on equal pieces make a fair ingredient test.

activities.prompt: Natural dye can colour clothes and pots. Can it also colour recycled paper?
options: Yes, natural dye can colour recycled paper.
No, natural dye can colour only clothes and pots.
No, recycled paper can use only artificial dye.
Yes, but only clothes can use natural dye.

why.No, natural dye can colour only clothes: This limits natural dye to two uses and ignores its use on paper.
why.No, recycled paper can use only artifici: This confuses paper's allowed dyes by leaving out natural dye.
why.Yes, but only clothes can use natural dy: This wrongly limits natural dye to clothes and ignores pots.

activities.explanation: Paper can be painted with natural dyes, including recycled paper.

lessons.title: Paper in Books and Other Materials

activities.prompt: What surprising stories can books and other materials tell us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Paper and Other Materials
activities.body: Book paper is made from wood. The wood becomes pulp during paper making. The steps are similar to those for recycled paper. Making paper needs many trees, water and energy. We should use paper and other materials responsibly. Earlier, people wrote on cloth, leaves and wooden boards. People in India also used palm leaves called talapatra. Banana fibre can make environment-friendly paper. Alternative materials save trees and protect the environment.
keyPoints: Book paper is made from wood in the making of pulp.
Earlier people wrote on cloth, leaves and wooden boards.
Responsible use helps protect trees and the environment.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how paper is made and why we should use materials responsibly.

activities.prompt: A school needs book paper. Should it choose wood or banana fibre?
steps: Book paper starts with wood pulp, so making it needs many trees.
Making paper needs water and energy, so paper must be used carefully.
Banana fibre can make paper and save trees, protecting the environment.
The school should choose banana-fibre paper and use it responsibly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the paper used in books made from?
options: wood
cloth
palm leaves
banana fibre
activities.explanation: The wood is used to make pulp for book paper.

activities.prompt: In earlier times, people wrote on cloth, leaves and wooden boards.
activities.explanation: These were some materials used for writing in earlier times.

activities.prompt: What were the palm leaves used in India called?
options: pulp
banana fibre
talapatra
recycled paper
activities.explanation: People in India used palm leaves called talapatra.

activities.prompt: People in earlier times wrote on cloth, ______ and wooden boards.
activities.hint: This material grows outside and was also used for writing.
activities.explanation: Cloth, leaves and wooden boards were used for writing in earlier times.

activities.prompt: Match each material with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Cloth was written on earlier, talapatra was used in India, and banana fibre can make paper.

activities.prompt: Which benefit can alternative materials give?
options: They save trees and protect the environment.
They make book paper unlike recycled paper.
They remove the need for water and energy.
They make responsible use unnecessary.
activities.explanation: Banana fibre is one alternative material that can save trees and protect the environment.

activities.prompt: A child draws on one notebook page. What should the child do next?
options: Keep the page and draw on its other side.
Throw away the page after one small drawing.
Take a new page for the next small drawing.
Tear out several pages before drawing again.

why.Throw away the page after one small draw: This treats one use as enough and wastes paper.
why.Take a new page for the next small drawi: This uses a fresh page for each drawing and wastes more paper.
why.Tear out several pages before drawing ag: This tears out extra paper without a need.

activities.explanation: Keeping and reusing the page uses the paper responsibly.

activities.prompt: A shop changes from wooden-paper bags to banana-fibre bags. What will likely happen to the need for trees?
options: Fewer trees will be needed because banana fibre saves trees.
More trees will be needed because the shop will make more bags.
The same trees will be needed because banana fibre is still paper.
No trees will be needed because banana fibre is environment-friendly.

why.More trees will be needed because the sh: This mistakes a material change for more bags being made.
why.The same trees will be needed because ba: This assumes all paper still comes from wood.
why.No trees will be needed because banana f: This mistakes environment-friendly for needing no trees at all.

activities.explanation: This is right because banana fibre saves trees.

activities.prompt: A town makes more book paper from wood pulp. What will likely happen to its needs?
options: It will need more trees, water, and energy.
It will need more trees, but less water and energy.
It will need more water, but fewer trees and energy.
It will need more energy, but fewer trees and water.

why.It will need more trees, but less water: This wrongly assumes more paper needs less water and energy.
why.It will need more water, but fewer trees: This wrongly assumes wood pulp needs fewer trees.
why.It will need more energy, but fewer tree: This wrongly assumes wood pulp needs fewer trees and water.

activities.explanation: This is right because more paper needs more wood, water, and energy.

activities.prompt: A learner wants to test how two paper types are made. Which check is fairest?
options: Compare the making steps for both kinds of paper.
Compare only the final sizes of both paper sheets.
Guess how one paper is made without checking its steps.
Compare colours first and ignore both making steps.

why.Compare only the final sizes of both pap: This compares an outcome instead of the making steps.
why.Guess how one paper is made without chec: This uses a guess instead of checking both processes.
why.Compare colours first and ignore both ma: This ignores the steps that the test should compare.

activities.explanation: This is fair because it compares the making steps of both types.

lessons.title: Kinds of Paper and Their Uses

activities.prompt: Which kind of paper would you choose for each job?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Paper for Every Purpose
activities.body: We use writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard and tissue paper. Different types of paper suit different purposes. Tissue paper is thin and soft. It absorbs water and is useful for cleaning. Cardboard is thick and hard. It makes boxes for packing objects.
keyPoints: Different papers have different uses.
Tissue paper is useful for cleaning.
Cardboard makes boxes for packing objects.
activities.explanation: Each kind of paper has special qualities for different jobs.

activities.prompt: A child must clean a wet table. The child also needs a box for packing objects. Which paper fits each job?
steps: Tissue paper absorbs water, so it can clean the wet table.
Cardboard makes boxes for packing objects, so it fits the box job.
Different paper types suit different purposes because their qualities differ.
Use tissue paper for the table and cardboard for the box.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Paper for Cleaning
activities.prompt: Which paper is used for cleaning?
options: writing paper
art paper
cardboard
tissue paper
activities.explanation: Tissue paper is used for cleaning. It is thin and soft.

activities.title: Match Paper with Its Use
activities.prompt: Match each item with the correct detail.
activities.explanation: Tissue paper cleans, cardboard packs objects, and Braille patterns form tiny bumps.

activities.title: Packing with Cardboard
activities.prompt: Cardboard is used to make ______ for packing objects.
activities.hint: Think of a strong container for toys.
activities.explanation: Cardboard is thick and hard. These qualities make it useful for packing boxes.

activities.title: A Special Quality
activities.prompt: Which detail about tissue paper is true?
options: A hard and thick sheet.
A sheet that absorbs water.
A sheet full of bumps.
A sheet used for packing.
activities.explanation: Tissue paper absorbs water. This helps it work well for cleaning.

activities.title: Who Does Braille Help?
activities.prompt: Who does Braille help to read and write?
options: People who pack objects
People who clean spills
People who fold newspaper
Visually challenged people
activities.explanation: Braille helps visually challenged people to read and write.

activities.title: What Braille Represents
activities.prompt: Braille patterns represent numbers, alphabets and ______.
activities.hint: These marks help show pauses and question marks.
activities.explanation: Braille patterns can represent numbers, alphabets and punctuation.

activities.prompt: Tissue paper is used for cleaning and absorbs water. Cardboard is thick and hard. Which paper should wipe the wet table, and why?
options: Use tissue paper because it absorbs water.
Use cardboard because it absorbs water.
Use tissue paper because it is soft.
Use cardboard because it is hard.

This mistake gives cardboard the absorbing quality of tissue paper.
This mistake uses softness alone and ignores water absorption.
This mistake thinks hardness helps wipe away water.

activities.explanation: This is right because tissue paper absorbs water and is used for cleaning.

activities.prompt: Cardboard makes boxes for packing objects. Tissue paper is used for cleaning. A child needs packing boxes. Which choice and reason fits?
options: Choose cardboard because it makes packing boxes.
Choose tissue because it makes packing boxes.
Choose tissue because it absorbs water.
Choose cardboard because it is soft.

why.Choose tissue because it makes packing b: This mistake gives tissue paper the box-making use of cardboard.
This mistake chooses tissue for packing because it absorbs water.
This mistake reverses cardboard's hard quality.

activities.explanation: This is right because cardboard is used to make boxes for packing objects.

activities.prompt: Tissue paper absorbs water. Cardboard is thick and hard. Which test best compares how the papers handle water?
options: Put equal water on each paper, then compare.
Touch each paper, then choose the softest.
Use one tissue paper and many cardboards.
Soak each paper for a different time.

why.Touch each paper, then choose the softes: This mistake compares softness instead of water handling.
why.Use one tissue paper and many cardboards: This mistake gives the papers different amounts of paper.
This mistake changes the soaking times, so the test is not fair.

activities.explanation: This is fair because both papers receive equal water.

lessons.sceneCaption: A large, sturdy cardboard box shows how cardboard is used for packing.

lessons.title: The 5Rs and Creative Paper Use

activities.prompt: What could you make from paper you were about to throw away?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the 5Rs
activities.body: The 5Rs are five steps that can help us reduce waste. Refuse means saying no to things that make waste. Reduce means using things carefully and making less waste. Reuse means using something many times. Repurpose means using something in a new, creative way. Recycle means using steps to turn a thing into something new. Used paper can become many useful and creative things.
keyPoints: Refuse, reduce, reuse, repurpose and recycle help us reduce waste.
Each 5R gives a different way to handle waste.
Used paper can become useful and creative things.
activities.explanation: The 5Rs give you many ways to waste less paper.

activities.prompt: An old newspaper is unused. What can a child make from it?
steps: Do not throw it away, because used paper can make useful things.
Make a toy or decoration, because old newspapers can make both.
This is Repurpose, because the newspaper gets a new and creative use.
So make something new, because small changes can save resources and reduce pollution.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which action shows the 5R called refuse?
options: Using something many times
Using things carefully
Saying no to wasteful things
Turning waste into something new
activities.explanation: Refuse means saying no to things that make waste. You have spotted it!

activities.prompt: How can old newspapers be used in a new, creative way?
options: To make toys and decorations
To make single-use paper cups
To make more notes on one side
To make waste on both sides
activities.explanation: Old newspapers can be repurposed into toys and decorations. That is creative!

activities.prompt: Match each 5R with its meaning.
pairs: Say no to things that make waste
Use things carefully and make less waste
Use something in a new, creative way
Use steps to turn a thing into something new
activities.explanation: You matched all five ways of reducing waste. Nicely done!

activities.prompt: Recycle means using ______ to turn a thing into something new.
activities.hint: Think about what happens before a thing becomes new.
activities.explanation: Recycling uses steps to turn a thing into something new. Well done!

activities.prompt: Which paper habit can help reduce waste?
options: Use both sides for notes
Use one side then discard it
Choose single-use paper cups
Throw old newspapers away
activities.explanation: Using both sides of paper makes less waste. This is a smart 5R choice!

activities.prompt: Put the five steps of the waste plan in order.
activities.explanation: The five steps are refuse, reduce, reuse, repurpose and recycle. You found the full plan!

activities.prompt: Refusing single-use paper cups means saying no to things that make waste. What will happen if a family refuses them?
options: Less paper will become waste.
More paper will become waste.
The cups will become decorations.
The cups will become new paper.

It treats refusing as if it invited more waste.
It mixes Refuse with Repurpose; refusing does not remake cups.
It mixes Refuse with Recycle; refusing does not remake cups.

activities.explanation: Refusing single-use cups directly reduces this source of waste.

activities.prompt: Using both sides of paper for notes makes less waste. What is likely to happen to paper use?
options: Paper will be saved because less waste is made.
Paper will be wasted because notes need one side.
Paper will become toys because notes are finished.
Paper will stay unused because notes need one side.

why.Paper will be wasted because notes need: It wrongly assumes every note sheet must have one unused side.
why.Paper will become toys because notes are: It mixes Reduce with Repurpose; reducing waste does not make toys.
why.Paper will stay unused because notes nee: It confuses saving paper with leaving paper unused.

activities.explanation: Small changes can save resources and reduce waste.

activities.prompt: Using both sides of paper can make less waste. Which test is fairest for checking this?
options: Compare sheets needed for the same notes on one or two sides.
Compare toys made from one or two old newspapers.
Compare cups used before and after refusing paper cups.
Compare notes drawn on one or two paper sides.

why.Compare toys made from one or two old ne: This changes the test from paper saving to making toys.
why.Compare cups used before and after refus: This tests Refuse instead of Reduce.
why.Compare notes drawn on one or two paper: This counts notes, not how much paper is needed.

activities.explanation: This keeps the notes the same and changes only the paper sides used.

activities.prompt: Using both sides of paper for notes makes less waste. A child calls this Reuse. What is wrong with the claim?
options: Using both sides mainly reduces waste by using paper carefully.
Using both sides mainly reuses paper for a new purpose.
Using both sides mainly changes paper into something new.
Using both sides mainly stops paper cups from being used.

why.Using both sides mainly reuses paper for: It mixes Reduce with Repurpose; a new purpose changes the meaning.
why.Using both sides mainly changes paper in: It mixes Reduce with Recycle; paper is not changed into something new.
why.Using both sides mainly stops paper cups: It mixes Reduce with Refuse; no single-use cup is involved.

activities.explanation: Using both sides is Reduce because careful use makes less waste.

activities.prompt: Refusing single-use cups and using both sides of paper are small changes. What result can a class expect?
options: The environment is helped, and resources can be saved.
The environment is hurt, and resources can be wasted.
The environment is helped, but resources cannot be saved.
The environment is hurt, but resources can be saved.

why.The environment is hurt, and resources c: It reverses what small changes can do for the environment and resources.
why.The environment is helped, but resources: It wrongly separates helping the environment from saving resources.
why.The environment is hurt, but resources c: It gets the environment effect wrong, but the resource effect right.

activities.explanation: Small changes can help the environment and save resources.

activities.context: Pihu holds her drawing book and looks at a newspaper. She saw a picture of trees on the newspaper's front page. Beside them sits a pot whose surface looks like paper, although it feels rough unlike Pihu's drawing book. Pihu learns that the pot is made from recycled paper. She asks whether they can make paper like the pot's. This makes her think about how paper is connected with trees and why recycling it can help save them.
activities.prompt: If people recycle more paper, what result should Pihu expect?
options: Trees could be saved.
Trees might be cut down to make more new paper.
Trees might be used up more quickly.
Trees might grow more slowly because more paper is made.

why.Trees might be cut down to make more new: Making more new paper can require more trees.
Faster use of trees would not save them.
why.Trees might grow more slowly because mor: Recycling does not make trees grow more slowly.

activities.explanation: Recycling paper helps save trees.

activities.context: Pihu holds her drawing book and looks at a newspaper. She saw a picture of trees on the newspaper's front page. Beside them sits a pot whose surface looks like paper, although it feels rough unlike Pihu's drawing book. Pihu learns that the pot is made from recycled paper. She asks whether they can make paper like the pot's. This makes her think about how paper is connected with trees and why recycling it can help save them.
activities.prompt: Which idea best explains why Pihu can make paper like the pot's while also helping trees?
options: Paper comes from trees, and using recycled paper helps save them.
Paper comes from trees, but using recycled paper does not help trees.
Paper does not come from trees, so recycling it cannot help them.
Paper looks like the pot's, so its texture determines its effect on trees.

why.Paper does not come from trees, so recyc: Trees are the source of paper.
why.Paper looks like the pot's, so its textu: A paper-like appearance does not explain its connection with trees.

activities.explanation: Paper is made from trees.

activities.prompt: Explain how paper is connected with trees and why recycling paper helps save trees.
activities.answer: Paper is made from trees, so trees provide the material for it. When paper is recycled, it can be used again, so fewer trees need to be cut down. Recycling paper therefore helps save trees.
points: Paper is made from trees.
Recycled paper can be used again.
Fewer trees may need to be cut down.
Recycling helps save trees.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is making recycled paper. The student has old newspapers, fenugreek seeds, and water. The newspapers are torn into small pieces and soaked in water. A small quantity of fenugreek seeds is added, and the mixture is left overnight. The next day, the student blends the soaked paper and seeds with a grinder, making a wet mixture. The paste is spread on a flat base and rolled into thin sheets. The student leaves the sheets to dry.
activities.prompt: After the student blends the soaked paper and seeds, what should the student do next?
options: Place the wet mixture on a flat surface, shape it into thin sheets, and let it dry.
Leave the blended mixture in its container until it dries.
Dry the soaked paper pieces before spreading them.
Add more water and leave the mixture overnight again.

why.Leave the blended mixture in its contain: The mixture must first be spread and rolled into thin sheets.
why.Dry the soaked paper pieces before sprea: The soaked mixture should be shaped into sheets before it dries.
why.Add more water and leave the mixture ove: This repeats a preparation step instead of making sheets.

activities.explanation: This is the correct step after making the wet mixture.

activities.prompt: Explain why fenugreek seeds are added when making recycled paper.
activities.answer: The fenugreek seeds are added because they act as a binding material. They help the wet paper mixture hold together when it is spread and rolled into thin sheets. This binding helps the sheets keep their shape as they dry into recycled paper.
points: Fenugreek seeds are added to the soaked paper.
The seeds act as a binding material.
The binding helps the paper mixture hold together.
The mixture is spread, rolled, and dried after this.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After making recycled paper, a student brings the sheet to class. The class plans to cut it into equal-sized pieces, colour the pieces with natural ingredients from a table, and record what they notice. One student uses leaves for a natural dye. Another asks whether a dye made from roots could also be used. The class wants each piece to receive an equal share of the colouring ingredient and wants to colour and design the recycled paper.
activities.prompt: Before colouring, what should the class do with the sheet of recycled paper?
options: Divide it into pieces of equal size.
Keep it whole and colour only its surface.
Cut it into pieces of different sizes.
Colour it first and cut it afterwards.

why.Keep it whole and colour only its surfac: The paper should be cut before the pieces are coloured.
Different-sized pieces do not follow the activity.
The class should cut the paper before colouring the pieces.

activities.explanation: The paper must be divided into pieces of the same size.

activities.context: After making recycled paper, a student brings the sheet to class. The class plans to cut it into equal-sized pieces, colour the pieces with natural ingredients from a table, and record what they notice. One student uses leaves for a natural dye. Another asks whether a dye made from roots could also be used. The class wants each piece to receive an equal share of the colouring ingredient and wants to colour and design the recycled paper.
activities.prompt: The student wants to make another natural dye from roots instead of leaves. What should the student expect?
options: The roots can provide a natural dye.
Only leaves can provide a natural dye.
The roots would make an artificial dye.
The roots cannot provide a natural dye.

Natural dyes can come from several plant parts, not only leaves.
A dye made from roots is natural because roots are a plant part.
Roots are included among the plant parts used for natural dyes.

activities.explanation: Roots are among the plant parts used to make natural dyes.

activities.prompt: How should the class colour and design the recycled paper, and what should they write down?
activities.answer: The class should cut the recycled paper into equal-sized pieces. They should colour the pieces using natural ingredients from the table and the same quantity for every piece. Other natural ingredients can also be used. They should write down their observations in the table and add designs to the paper.
points: Paper is cut into pieces of the same size.
Natural ingredients from the table are used.
Every piece receives the same quantity.
Observations are recorded and designs are added.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A class is preparing a new book and needs paper for its pages. The children learn that ordinary book paper is made from wood that is turned into pulp. They also learn that making paper needs many trees, much water and much energy. A student suggests banana fibre because it can be used to make paper and is environment-friendly. Another student worries that choosing paper responsibly will help protect trees and the environment.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the class used banana-fibre paper instead of wood-pulp paper for its book?
options: It would reduce the number of trees needed for the book's pages.
It would make the book's production require more water and energy.
It would protect trees even if making the paper used much more water and energy.
It would mean that paper-making no longer needs trees in any other book.

why.It would make the book's production requ: The facts do not show that this choice requires more water and energy.
why.It would protect trees even if making th: Protecting trees does not depend on using extra water and energy.
why.It would mean that paper-making no longe: One book's choice would not remove tree needs for all other paper-making.

activities.explanation: Banana-fibre paper can save trees and protect the environment.

activities.context: A class is preparing a new book and needs paper for its pages. The children learn that ordinary book paper is made from wood that is turned into pulp. They also learn that making paper needs many trees, much water and much energy. A student suggests banana fibre because it can be used to make paper and is environment-friendly. Another student worries that choosing paper responsibly will help protect trees and the environment.
activities.prompt: Why does making book paper from wood pulp have an effect on the environment?
options: Because the trees are needed only to colour the pages.
Because water and energy are needed only for materials made from banana fibre.
Because its production uses many trees and substantial amounts of water and energy.
Because making wood pulp requires no water or energy.

why.Because the trees are needed only to col: This confuses wood pulp with an environment-friendly alternative.
why.Because water and energy are needed only: Water and energy are needed for making paper generally, not only banana-fibre paper.
why.Because making wood pulp requires no wat: Making paper does need both water and energy.

activities.explanation: Making book paper uses wood, many trees, much water and much energy.

activities.prompt: Explain why making and using book paper responsibly matters.
activities.answer: Making book paper uses wood to make pulp, and it needs many trees, much water and energy. Because these materials are needed, we should use paper and other materials responsibly. Choosing environment-friendly alternatives such as banana fibre can save trees and protect the environment.
points: Book paper is made from wood turned into pulp.
Making paper needs many trees, much water and energy.
Paper and other materials should be used responsibly.
Alternatives such as banana fibre can save trees and protect the environment.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A person is packing objects. They choose cardboard because it is thick and hard, and it is used to make boxes. Later, a surface needs cleaning, so the person uses tissue paper. Tissue paper is thin and soft, and it absorbs water. A person who is visually challenged is also given Braille paper. Braille patterns can be felt as tiny bumps, and they represent numbers, alphabets and punctuation, helping the person read and write.
activities.prompt: In the case, which material should be used to make a box for packing objects?
options: The thick, hard material
The thin, soft material
The material that absorbs water
The material with tiny bumps

why.The thin, soft material: Thin and soft describes tissue paper, not box material.
why.The material that absorbs water: Absorbing water is a tissue-paper property.
why.The material with tiny bumps: Tiny bumps belong to Braille patterns, not box-making.

activities.explanation: This matches the need for a thick, hard box material.

activities.context: A person is packing objects. They choose cardboard because it is thick and hard, and it is used to make boxes. Later, a surface needs cleaning, so the person uses tissue paper. Tissue paper is thin and soft, and it absorbs water. A person who is visually challenged is also given Braille paper. Braille patterns can be felt as tiny bumps, and they represent numbers, alphabets and punctuation, helping the person read and write.
activities.prompt: If the Braille patterns on the paper could not be felt as bumps, which ability would be affected?
options: The ability to read and write using Braille.
The ability to absorb water during cleaning.
The ability to make a box for packing objects.
The ability to use a thin, soft material for cleaning.

why.The ability to absorb water during clean: Water absorption is a property of tissue paper.
why.The ability to make a box for packing ob: Boxes for packing objects are made from cardboard.
why.The ability to use a thin, soft material: Cleaning is the purpose of tissue paper.

activities.explanation: Braille patterns that can be felt help people read and write.

activities.prompt: Explain why different types of paper are used for different purposes.
activities.answer: Cardboard and tissue paper have different qualities and uses. Cardboard is thick and hard, so it is used to make boxes for packing objects. Tissue paper is thin, soft, and absorbs water, so it is used for cleaning. This shows that different types of paper are chosen for different purposes.
points: Cardboard is thick and hard.
Cardboard is used to make boxes for packing objects.
Tissue paper is thin and soft.
Tissue paper is used for cleaning and absorbs water.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At home, a student noticed that the family was throwing away lots of paper. The student suggested refusing single-use paper cups and using both sides of paper for notes. The student also kept old newspapers and used them to make toys and decorations. The family was pleased because the toys were useful, and the changes helped the environment, saved resources and reduced pollution. The student made a small plan for using paper more carefully.
activities.prompt: The student wants to make a new toy from old newspapers. Which 5R best describes this action?
options: Repurpose
Refuse
Reduce
Recycle

why.Refuse: This wrongly suggests saying no to the newspapers.
why.Reduce: This wrongly suggests using them carefully to make less waste.
why.Recycle: This confuses changing the creative use with using steps to turn something into something new.

activities.explanation: This uses something in a new and creative way.

activities.context: At home, a student noticed that the family was throwing away lots of paper. The student suggested refusing single-use paper cups and using both sides of paper for notes. The student also kept old newspapers and used them to make toys and decorations. The family was pleased because the toys were useful, and the changes helped the environment, saved resources and reduced pollution. The student made a small plan for using paper more carefully.
activities.prompt: What should the student expect after using both sides of paper for notes?
options: Less paper will be needed for notes, so less waste will be made.
More paper will be needed because each side requires a separate sheet.
The amount of paper waste will stay the same because both sides make no difference.
No waste will be made because writing notes is the same as refusing things.

why.More paper will be needed because each s: This is a mistake about how the two sides can be used.
why.The amount of paper waste will stay the: This wrongly denies that careful use can reduce waste.
why.No waste will be made because writing no: This confuses reducing waste with refusing it.

activities.explanation: Using both sides carefully makes less paper waste.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between refusing and reducing waste.
activities.answer: Refusing means saying no to things that make waste, such as single-use paper cups. Reducing means using things carefully so that less waste is made, such as writing notes on both sides of one sheet of paper.
points: Defines refusing correctly.
Gives the paper cup example.
Defines reducing correctly.
Gives the both-sides paper example.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: How Things are Made

activities.title: The Paper Pot
activities.prompt: Which material is the pot made from?
options: Banana fibre
Recycled paper
Fenugreek seeds
Palm leaves
activities.explanation: The pot is made from recycled paper.

activities.title: The Binding Material
activities.prompt: The seeds added to the paper mixture act as the ______ material.
activities.hint: What holds the mixture together?
activities.explanation: Fenugreek seeds act as a binding material.

activities.title: Making Recycled Paper
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order to make recycled paper.
items: Tear the newspapers into small pieces and soak them in water.
Add fenugreek seeds and leave the mixture overnight.
Blend or mash the soaked paper and fenugreek seeds.
Spread the paste on a flat base and roll it into thin sheets.
activities.explanation: The process moves from soaking the paper to drying the thin sheets.

activities.title: Natural Dyes
activities.prompt: Where do natural dyes come from?
options: Trees in the making of pulp
Paper and water
Different parts of plants
Cloth and wooden boards
activities.explanation: Natural dyes are made from different parts of plants.

activities.title: Packing with Cardboard
activities.prompt: Cardboard is used to make ______ for packing objects.
activities.hint: Cardboard is thick and hard.
activities.explanation: Cardboard is used to make boxes for packing objects.

activities.title: The 5Rs of Waste Management
activities.prompt: Match each waste-management step with its meaning.
pairs: saying no to things that make waste
using things carefully to make less waste
using something many times before throwing it away
using something in a new and creative way
turning a thing into something new
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a waste-management step with its meaning.

activities.title: Two Kinds of Paper
activities.prompt: The steps for making book paper are similar to those for recycled paper.
activities.explanation: Both kinds of paper have similar making steps.

activities.title: An Alternative Material
activities.prompt: Which material is environment-friendly and can be used to make paper?
options: Cardboard
Newspaper
Tissue paper
Banana fibre
activities.explanation: Banana fibre is environment-friendly and can be used to make paper.

chapters.title: Our Environment
chapters.summary: In this chapter: back to school from holidays; in the land of agriculture, with gurpreet; in the land of endless sand, with ritika; on the seashore, with chandni.

lessons.title: Back to School from Holidays

activities.prompt: How do holiday stories help us discover the world around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Holiday stories and different places
activities.body: Children returned to school excited to talk about their holidays. Colourful pictures and other visit items filled their desks. The teacher invited everyone to share holiday experiences. Children spoke about beaches, deserts, grandparents and mountains. These places have different natural setups. Nature and culture are closely connected.
keyPoints: Children shared stories about their holidays.
Their visits included different kinds of places.
Nature helps shape how people live.
activities.explanation: Holiday stories help us learn about different places and their nature.

activities.prompt: A child sees holiday pictures from two regions. Why might life differ?
steps: The desert and coastal region have different natural setups.
Different natural setups shape life because each place has different surroundings.
Nature and culture are closely connected, so culture also depends on nature.
Therefore, each region’s life may reflect its own nature.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What filled the desks?
activities.prompt: What did colourful pictures and other visit items fill?
options: The children's desks
The teacher's books
The classroom windows
The school garden
activities.explanation: Colourful pictures and other items from visits filled the children's desks.

activities.title: Chandni's holiday visit
activities.prompt: Where did Chandni visit during her holiday?
options: A beach in Odisha
A desert in Rajasthan
The mountains of Sikkim
Her grandparents in Amritsar
activities.explanation: Chandni told the class about visiting a beach in Odisha.

activities.title: Match the child and visit
activities.prompt: Match each child with the place they described.
activities.explanation: Each child shared a story about a different place or family visit.

activities.title: Nayan's special visit
activities.prompt: Nayan described his visit to the majestic ______ of Sikkim.
activities.hint: Think of the tall landforms in Sikkim.
activities.explanation: Nayan described his visit to the majestic mountains of Sikkim.

activities.title: Nature and everyday life
activities.prompt: Which statement about a place's natural setup is correct?
options: Natural setup shapes how people live.
Natural setup shapes only the weather.
Natural setup shapes only what plants grow.
Natural setup shapes places, never people.
activities.explanation: The natural setup of a place helps shape how people live.

activities.title: A close connection
activities.prompt: Which connection does the lesson highlight?
options: Nature and culture are closely connected.
Nature and culture never affect each other.
Nature matters only in one kind of place.
Culture matters only during holidays.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows that nature and culture are closely connected.

activities.prompt: Pictures and visit items fill the desks. What will the teacher do next?
options: Invite children to share holiday experiences.
Ask children to hide every holiday item.
Invite children to forget their visits.
Ask children to leave the classroom.

This mistakes sharing for hiding the children’s memories.
This mistakes sharing for forgetting the holiday visits.
This mistakes an invitation to share for asking children to leave.

activities.explanation: This follows the teacher’s invitation to share holiday experiences.

activities.prompt: Desert and coastal holidays are compared. What should the class expect?
options: Their natural setups will become exactly the same.
Their natural setups may shape different ways of living.
Their culture will stop being connected to nature.
Their holiday pictures will show no visits.

why.Their natural setups will become exactly: This wrongly assumes different places have the same natural setup.
why.Their culture will stop being connected: This wrongly treats nature and culture as separate.
why.Their holiday pictures will show no visi: This wrongly assumes pictures can erase actual visits.

activities.explanation: Different natural setups can shape different ways of living.

activities.prompt: The class compares different kinds of regions. Which plan is fairest?
options: Ask only one region about nature.
Use different questions for each region.
Ask similar questions in every region.
Choose the region with nicest pictures.

Asking only one region cannot make a fair comparison.
Different questions can change answers because the words are different.
Nice pictures are not a fair measure of holiday experiences.

activities.explanation: Similar questions give every region the same chance.

activities.prompt: A beach visit proves all regions are alike. What mistake is this?
options: A beach visit proves every region shares the same culture.
A beach visit proves nature and culture are separate.
A beach visit means all regions have one natural setup.
A beach visit cannot represent every region.

why.A beach visit proves every region shares: This confuses one place’s culture with every region’s culture.
why.A beach visit proves nature and culture: This wrongly treats a single visit as proof of separation.
why.A beach visit means all regions have one: This repeats the mistake of generalising from one beach.

activities.explanation: A beach visit cannot represent every region’s natural setup.

activities.prompt: Nature and culture are linked. What may change when nature changes?
options: Local culture will surely stay unchanged.
All places will gain one natural setup.
Local living and culture may change together.
Nature will become separate from culture.

why.Local culture will surely stay unchanged: This wrongly assumes close connection means culture never changes.
This wrongly assumes all places share one natural setup.
why.Nature will become separate from culture: This wrongly assumes connection means nature and culture are separate.

activities.explanation: Close connection means nature can shape both living and culture.
