activities.context: During the morning, a student looked outside and saw an orange sky. Later, the student noticed that the sky’s colour had changed and that the Sun also seemed to have a different colour. The student remembered that the chapter asked for observations in the morning, afternoon and at night. The student planned to observe again at those times and share the observations with classmates so they could compare what they had seen.
activities.prompt: If the student observes the sky again in the afternoon, what should the student expect?
options: The sky may have a different colour from the orange morning sky.
The sky must stay orange until night begins.
The sky will look exactly the same because its colour does not change.
The sky will always have the same colour as the Sun.

why.The sky must stay orange until night beg: The colour does not have to remain the same as in the morning.
why.The sky will look exactly the same becau: The sky does change, so it may not look exactly the same.
why.The sky will always have the same colour: The sky and the Sun can show different colours.

activities.explanation: The sky’s colour changes during the morning, afternoon and night.

activities.context: During the morning, a student looked outside and saw an orange sky. Later, the student noticed that the sky’s colour had changed and that the Sun also seemed to have a different colour. The student remembered that the chapter asked for observations in the morning, afternoon and at night. The student planned to observe again at those times and share the observations with classmates so they could compare what they had seen.
activities.prompt: What should the student do so that classmates can compare sky observations at different times?
options: Observe in the morning, afternoon and at night, then share the observations.
Observe only in the morning and keep the observations private.
Share only the orange morning sky and do not observe again.
Wait until all the animals behave differently before observing anything.

why.Observe only in the morning and keep the: Sharing allows classmates to compare their observations.
why.Share only the orange morning sky and do: Other times of the day must also be observed.
why.Wait until all the animals behave differ: The comparison should focus on observations of the sky.

activities.explanation: The chapter asks for observations in the morning, afternoon and at night.

activities.prompt: Why can the sky and the Sun look different at different times of the day?
activities.answer: The sky can look different because its colour changes during the morning, afternoon and night. The Sun’s colour also seems to change. These changes can make the whole view of the sky look different at different times of the day.
points: The sky’s colour changes during the day.
The morning, afternoon and night are included.
The Sun’s colour also seems to change.
Different times can produce a different sky view.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student looks out of the window in the morning and sees the Sun appear to rise. The Sun is the brightest and most visible object in the sky, and its light and heat can be felt. As the student watches, the Sun seems to move upwards until it comes overhead. Later, it appears to move downwards towards the other side of the sky, before it eventually disappears from view.
activities.prompt: After the Sun comes overhead, what should the student expect to happen next?
options: It will seem to move lower and eventually go out of sight.
It will seem to climb even higher.
It will stay directly overhead without changing position.
It will begin its upward journey again.

Wrong: moving upwards happens before it comes overhead.
why.It will stay directly overhead without c: Wrong: its apparent position changes after it comes overhead.
Wrong: the upward movement belongs to the earlier part of the journey.

activities.explanation: Correct: the later journey is downwards before it disappears.

activities.context: A student looks out of the window in the morning and sees the Sun appear to rise. The Sun is the brightest and most visible object in the sky, and its light and heat can be felt. As the student watches, the Sun seems to move upwards until it comes overhead. Later, it appears to move downwards towards the other side of the sky, before it eventually disappears from view.
activities.prompt: What should the student do to watch the whole visible journey of the Sun?
options: Keep watching its changing position until it is no longer visible.
Watch only the upward part and stop when the Sun reaches the middle.
Look away after the Sun appears because its position will not change.
Wait until the Sun disappears and then begin watching it rise.

why.Watch only the upward part and stop when: Wrong: this leaves out the later downward movement and disappearance.
why.Look away after the Sun appears because: Wrong: the Sun appears to change position throughout its visible journey.
why.Wait until the Sun disappears and then b: Wrong: this reverses the order of the visible journey.

activities.explanation: Correct: this follows the Sun from its appearance through to disappearance.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Sun’s visible journey changes from the morning until it disappears from view.
activities.answer: In the morning, the Sun appears to rise and seems to move upwards until it comes overhead. Later, it appears to move downwards towards the other side of the sky. Eventually, it disappears from view, completing the visible journey that we all enjoy watching.
points: It appears to rise in the morning.
It seems to move upwards until it comes overhead.
It later appears to move downwards.
It eventually disappears from view.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how the child's shadow changes during the day and when the child moves or changes pose.
activities.answer: The shadow is long in the morning, short at noon, and long again in the evening. Its evening direction is opposite to its morning direction. It also moves with the child, seems to run when the child runs, and changes shape when the child changes pose.
points: Morning shadows are long.
Noon shadows are short.
Evening shadows are long and point opposite to morning shadows.
Movement and pose changes affect how the shadow appears.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a dark room, a student pointed a torch at a stick and moved the stick back and forth. The shadow changed, and a stick closer to the torch made a bigger shadow. Changing the torchlight’s direction changed the shadow’s direction. Outside, the Sun appeared to move from the East to overhead by noon, then towards the West in the afternoon. This movement changed the shadow’s direction, so shadows could be used to find the time.
activities.prompt: If the student moves the stick closer to the torch, what should happen to the shadow?
options: It would grow smaller.
It would stay exactly the same size.
It would grow larger.
It would vanish entirely.

Moving closer would not make the shadow smaller.
Nothing in the experiment says that changing the distance leaves the size unchanged.
The torch still points at the stick, so the shadow would still be seen.

activities.explanation: An object close to the light source makes a bigger shadow.

activities.context: In a dark room, a student pointed a torch at a stick and moved the stick back and forth. The shadow changed, and a stick closer to the torch made a bigger shadow. Changing the torchlight’s direction changed the shadow’s direction. Outside, the Sun appeared to move from the East to overhead by noon, then towards the West in the afternoon. This movement changed the shadow’s direction, so shadows could be used to find the time.
activities.prompt: The student wants an instrument that can tell time accurately. Which should the student choose?
options: Samrat Yantra
The torch
The stick
The dark room

why.The torch: The torch is used to make and study shadows, not to tell time accurately.
why.The stick: The stick is the object that makes the shadow in the experiment.
why.The dark room: The dark room is where the shadow experiment takes place.

activities.explanation: Samrat Yantra is a sundial that can tell time accurately.

activities.prompt: Explain how moving the stick and changing the light direction affect the shadow in the torch experiment.
activities.answer: Pointing the torch at the stick makes a shadow that can be watched. Moving the stick closer to the torch makes the shadow bigger. Moving it back and forth lets the student observe changes. Changing the torchlight’s direction makes the shadow change direction.
points: The torch is pointed at the stick.
Moving the stick closer makes the shadow bigger.
Moving the stick back and forth helps observe shadow changes.
Changing the light direction changes the shadow direction.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After sunset, a child watched a shadow puppet show in India, where shadow puppetry has been practised for a long time. Outside, the sky dazzled with thousands of twinkling stars, and the child noticed different patterns among them. The Moon appeared to be the biggest object in the night sky. Its shape did not look the same on every night: once it looked like a complete circle, while on another night it could not be seen at all.
activities.prompt: While the shadow puppet show is happening after sunset, what should the child expect to see in the sky?
options: A night sky sparkling with thousands of stars
A night sky with no visible stars
A night sky whose stars make the same pattern on every night
A night sky with the Moon as its only visible object

why.A night sky with no visible stars: This contradicts the fact that the sky dazzles with stars.
why.A night sky whose stars make the same pa: The lesson says that different star patterns can be observed.
why.A night sky with the Moon as its only vi: This leaves out the thousands of stars in the sky.

activities.explanation: This matches the thousands of twinkling stars seen after sunset.

activities.context: After sunset, a child watched a shadow puppet show in India, where shadow puppetry has been practised for a long time. Outside, the sky dazzled with thousands of twinkling stars, and the child noticed different patterns among them. The Moon appeared to be the biggest object in the night sky. Its shape did not look the same on every night: once it looked like a complete circle, while on another night it could not be seen at all.
activities.prompt: If the child sees the Moon cut down the middle, which description fits that night's observation?
options: It appears split through the middle
It appears as a complete circle
It cannot be seen at all
It appears to be the biggest object in the sky

why.It appears as a complete circle: A complete circle is the appearance called Poornima.
why.It cannot be seen at all: An unseen new Moon is called Amavasya.
why.It appears to be the biggest object in t: Being the biggest object does not describe its split appearance.

activities.explanation: This describes the middle-cut appearance of the Moon.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Moon's appearance can be different on different nights.
activities.answer: On different nights, the Moon may look like a complete circle, like it has been cut down the middle, or it may not be visible at all. A complete circle is called Poornima, or the full Moon. The invisible new Moon is called Amavasya.
points: The Moon can look like a complete circle.
It can also look cut down the middle.
On some nights, the Moon cannot be seen.
Poornima and Amavasya are names for different appearances.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a family celebration, Neha noticed that there was no Moon in the sky. Her family explained that Diwali is celebrated at this time. Later, a full round Moon appeared. Her family said that Eid is celebrated when the Moon is visible, and specifically on the first night after a New Moon. Neha also read that India’s Vikram Lander landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023 and collected data about its surface.
activities.prompt: It is the night following a New Moon, and the Moon is visible. Which celebration matches this situation?
options: The celebration held on the night following a New Moon
The celebration held on a night with no visible Moon
The celebration held whenever the full round Moon appears
The celebration held on any night when the Moon is visible

why.The celebration held on a night with no: That celebration requires no Moon in the sky.
why.The celebration held whenever the full r: The full Moon is not identified as the first night after a New Moon.
why.The celebration held on any night when t: Any visible-Moon night is too broad because the New Moon timing is specified.

activities.explanation: This matches the first night following a New Moon.

activities.context: During a family celebration, Neha noticed that there was no Moon in the sky. Her family explained that Diwali is celebrated at this time. Later, a full round Moon appeared. Her family said that Eid is celebrated when the Moon is visible, and specifically on the first night after a New Moon. Neha also read that India’s Vikram Lander landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023 and collected data about its surface.
activities.prompt: Neha wants to explain why Vikram Lander’s work was useful for learning about the Moon. What is the best explanation?
options: It provided information about the Moon’s surface
It showed which festivals follow the New Moon
It explained how the full Moon changes shape
It revealed when people first began making calendars

why.It showed which festivals follow the New: Festival timing was not the purpose of collecting the data.
why.It explained how the full Moon changes s: The lesson connects festivals with the Moon’s appearance.
why.It revealed when people first began maki: The lander collected information about the surface, not calendar origins.

activities.explanation: The lander collected data about the Moon’s surface.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Moon’s appearance is connected with Diwali and Eid.
activities.answer: Diwali is celebrated when there is no Moon in the sky. Eid is celebrated on a day when the Moon is visible, specifically on the first night after a New Moon. Both festivals are linked to the Moon’s appearance, but their Moon conditions are different.
points: Links Diwali with a sky without the Moon
Links Eid with a visible Moon
Identifies the first night after a New Moon
Shows that the festivals have different Moon conditions
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.explanation: The sky changes colour during the morning, afternoon and night.

The stick bends
